Mr. E. J. GARLAND (Bow River) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, respecting the civil service (restoration of excluded positions) .
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?
No, no.

Mr. Speaker, I am frankly astonished at the number of refusals on the other side of the house to grant a second reading to this bill. In answer to your question "Shall the second reading of thei bill be carried?" there was quite a volume of "no" and that before the members who spoke had heard the argument thereon. I would take it, therefore, that they have pretty well made up their minds that in so far as patronage is now permitted they are going to cling to it with the tenacity of the party system of the older days. I hope, however, that after I have presented what few facts I have at my disposal on this matter, many of these same gentlemen will join with me in doing what they can to enforce and strengthen the principle as applied to our administrative service.
Order. I cannot hear the hon. member who is speaking.

I sympathize with Your Honour. Although my voice is by no means a loud one it can usually be heard.
After all there is one question the answer to which should determine our attitude totMr. Speaker.]
wards this whole problem and that is: Does Canada's public service need, efficient business supervision instead of political control as in the past? The answer to that will answer the whole problem in my opinion. This question has already been answered effectively and well in successive parliamentary reports on the civil service since 1877. From 1877 to 1924 successive commissions and committees have sat and discussed the whole problem, and in every case they have come to one definite conclusion, namely, that the merit system should be not only brought into effect but maintained properly in all its strength.
There is at the present time no provision for appeal and personal boards of welfare as in other democratic countries. That is another question and it is now being dealt with by a committee in another way; but there is another reason why the bill that I have before the house at the moment should carry and that is that, owing to a lack of proper supervision of the entire service, it is estimated that there is an annual loss to the country of more than $25,000,000 which could readily be saved if business management were permitted to apply.
Who estimates that?

I will give that in just a moment. In support of this latter statement several considerations may be mentioned. An annual saving of $746,000 alone has been effected by the government printing bureau under the readjustment by the Civil Service Commission. An annual saving of $860,000 has been achieved in the Post Office Department, partly by departmental economies, it is true, but partly also by adjustments made in the personnel by the Civil Service Commission. In the evidence adduced before the Spinney committee of 1921, Dr. Roche, a former minister of the interior, declared that an investigation of that department would reveal conditions similar to those in the printing bureau where a saving of thirty-seven per cent had been effected. If this is so, then more than a million dollars are beiing wasted in that department alone. The cost of the staff of the Interior department increased $1,500,000 from 1915 to 1922; it increased $1,000,000 from 1919 to 1922, which fact caused a protest by the way from Senator Bradbury in the Senate.
Similar references might be made concerning other departments. In one department there are several hundred men with expensive equipment lying idle, incurring an expenditure of nearly a million dollars. It is on record that the late John Fraser, when Auditor General, claimed more than once that the

Civil Service Act-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
Ottawa service was bearing an excessive overhead of 66 per cent. In the cost of maintaining the personnel at about $60,000,000, he estimated that a saving of 25 per cent or $15,000,000, at least, could be made. In public purchasing by open competition an estimated saving of thirty per cent on say $30,000,000, or $9,000,000 in all, could be effected and no mention is made of the losses on political contracts such as the Timiskam-ing dam, railways, merchant marine, and other matters.
What I have said might be extended almost without limit. For example, in ten parliamentary commissions on the civil service only once did the same person sit on two commissions and the same lack of continuity applies generally in the case of the history of civil service legislation introduced in this house since confederation. Then there is the extraordinary fact that though annually there is distributed in unnecessary expenditure more than $25,-
000.000, 19,000 civil servants receive on an average from $1,100 to $1,400, or slightly less in salaries.
One clause of my bill asks that the powers of the commission be extended. At the present time under the act the Civil Service Commission, although nominally having the power to go into and reorganize departments, in effect has not the power unless the deputy and other officials of the department consent, or invite the reorganization. That condition of affairs is wrong. It, should be compulsory upon the commission as part of its duties to enter into and reorganize the various departments of government consecutively, starting, if you like, with the largest and continuing through to the smallest. I say, as the result of what examination I have made of conditions, that if such a reorganization took place, if the commission undertook its duties properly and well, there would be a saving of even more than $20,000,000 a year in the administration of our civil service.
I am asking for the reinstatement under the commission of those positions that have been exempted by several orders in council, all but one of which were introduced by the present administration. When the present administration came into office practically the entire service was under the merit principle, but in the intervening years an enormous number of orders in council have been passed from time to time exempting various positions. In addition I am asking that departments that were regarded on their inauguration as temporary in nature, be now placed under the commission and given the rank of permanent. There is no reason I can see why they should not be so placed. The Prime Minister in his
recent speech on the budget stated that, having listened to the arguments of hon. members, there was no intention now of doing away with the income tax, and therefore we may assume that the income tax branch of the department will continue to exist. If it is going to continue to exist, then I ask, in fairness to the system and the staff of that branch, that they be placed under the commission and receive the advantages of the permanency of the staff and all the other recognitions that they would acquire under it.
The same thing is true with regard to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and the Soldier Settlement Board. Hon. members will remember that the argument at the outset for placing those departments outside of the operations of the act was that they were temporary, but ten years after the war we find they are still being maintained and in many cases the votes have been increased for those departments. There is therefore no indication at the present time of any temporary nature in those two departments. In fact recent speeches by hon. members would indicate clearly that we may regard the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment as being, at least in our lifetime, of a permanent nature. Then why should we not make it permanent and place it under the act? Hon. members will at once rise in opposition to this proposal of mine and say: How are you going to establish an effective test for the minor positions-the labourer, the postmaster of a small post office with a salary of less than $200 a year, and all that sort of thing? My answer to that is that other countries have done it and other countries are doing it effectively to-day. You will find throughout the world nations applying the principle which I am asking to be applied in this case to the very class of positions which this government saw fit to exempt under special orders in council.
It was not the government that exempted them, but the Civil Service Commission.

Ah well, the commission for some reason or other which we had better examine possibly before a committee of this house did, it is true, make some suggestions to the government with respect to that, but I say definitely to the government that if the ministers of the crown of that day had adhered to the principles which they themselves enunciated at an earlier date they would never have consented to the request of the commission, which was in my opinion an evasion of their proper

Civil Service Act-Air. Garland (Bow River)
responsibility and duty, and which had behind it unquestionably pressure from those who wanted to get back to the patronage system again. I do noit think you can escape that implication.
As a result of the abuses arising from patronage, including inefficiency, extravagance and abuses, the Union government some years ago placed under a special law, which I have under my hand, all civil service positions at that time; in other words, they provided that all positions in the service must be filled on the basis of open competition and of demonstrated ability to pa-form the work required. Those are almost the words of the act itself. As I have said, thousands of positions, some 13,000 odd, have since that time been exempted. The principal objection to retaining these positions under the Civil Service Commission was the impracticability of carrying on the proper examinations. When this question is discussed by hon. gentlemen opposite, and perhaps by one or two to my right, they will say that you cannot have an effective examination for these positions, and why should you have an examination at all for a labourer, for a man who works with a pick and shovel? My answer to that in the first place is that you can have an effective examination, and1 in the second place that the sustaining of the merit principle is so allimportant that no excuse on the ground of a temporary difficulty should be recognized as a binding reason why all these positions should be exempted'. We had a discussion in this house not long ago, a very heated and rather partisan one, with respect to the appointment of men to work on the retaining wall of the Rideau canal, and if the discussion that took place at that time is any criterion of the attitude of the public as a whole on this question, then what I have said stands well buttressed by the remarks of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning). At that time, if I remember aright, he intimated that so far as he was concerned he thought it would be better for all concerned, better for the members for Ottawa, better for himself and the government, and better for the men, that the commission should have the handling of these appointments. I refer you to bis words in Hansard of a few days ago.
Now the question arises, if you place these positions on the merit principle and make them subject to a civil service examination, no matter how perfunctory or casual it may be, some day or other you are going to be faced with the difficulty of making appointments, say, to the Public Works department in the city of Vancouver, and how are you going

to ask that branch in Vancouver or any other branch in a city far distant to wait until the Civil Service Commission in Ottawa has reter-mined whether it has men on the eligible list for that class of position? That is a difficulty that I have anticipated. I expect that will be one of the arguments that will be hurled against this bill, but my answer to that is that it is provided for in the act itself, in section 39, sub-sections 2 and 3, where it is provided:
When employees are required on short notice for emergency work outside the city of Ottawa a responsible agent or officer of the department requiring such extra assistance may engage the necessary employee and the said agent or officer in each case shall forthwith report to the commission through the deputy head of his department the names of the persons so employed.
And again:
No such employment shall extend beyond thirty days unless approved by the commission; but where the place of employment is outside the Dominion of Canada, the term of such employment may extend to ninety days.
Again:
Such employees may be paid the prevailing rate of pay at which persons qualified to perform such emergency work may be secured in the place or locality where the work is required to be done.
So that whole situation is carefully and studiously met by the provisions of the act itself. There is no difficulty, therefore, with respect to the making of temporary or emergency appointments in any part of the Dominion even if the Civil Service Commission is not at the moment in a position to make these appointments, because it is allowed thirty days, and an extension of time, if necessary, upon application from the deputy head of the department or the head of the works concerned.
I have in my hand evidence regarding the objections of council to the merit principle being applied in these exempted positions. A moment ago I intimated that the cabinet was responsible for the abandonment of the merit principle in this connection. When the commission reported to the government, the governor in council considered the situation, and then referred the matter back to the commission. On page 4 of the regulations you will find noted these words: "Considered too cumbersome and unnecessary, and the last step would be worse than the first." These words being interpreted to mean that the council did not agree to the merit regulation, and Dr. Roche says:
That was brought to our notice. When it came up in the formal board meeting, my colleagues-I give them credit for their own honest opinions-differed with me. I felt that

Civil Service Act-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
we had put that in all previous regulations, and I did not see why we should suddenly find out by a sudden conversion that this is not workable, and therefore I refused to sign a memo, without that being in, and I did it because of this fact.
That is the reason why I have included in my bill a provision tihat no position shall hereafter be excluded from the operation of the Civil Service Act of 1918 excepting upon the unanimous report of all the commissioners. There are only three of them, and the unanimous report of the three commissioners should be given. I find by examination of the reports of different committees and commissions examining into the civil service that in almost every case since the commission was established there has been a feeling that at least two of the commissioners have been to some extent influenced by those who would return to patronage, but there is one man to whom great credit is due who has at all times consistently refused to be swayed from the path of duty as 'laid down for him by the act itself, and that man is Dr. Roche. The greatest credit is due to him.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the other two commissioners were swayed from the path of duty?

No, not at all, but I feel that for reasons which they may very sincerely hold, they have listened perhaps at least with greater effect-we will put it that way-to the pressure from those who would return to patronage than Dr. Roche has. That is the way perhaps to put it. That is why I think, if the government is sincere in its desire to maintain the merit principle, it will at least insert this clause in the act, that no positions hereafter shall be excluded from the operation of the act excepting upon the unanimous report of the three commissioners. That is not asking too much; it is a fair provision. At the present time there is a strong suspicion which it would be well for the government to remove from the public mind and from the minds of hon. members of this house-it is no more than a suspicion, I grant you, but it is there and I have heard it in this house since I came here-that the last two appointees of this government to the Civil Service Commission are being motivated by the desire of the members of the party surrounding the Prime Minister in their actions with respect to these things.

Mr. Speaker,
my hon. friend is going a little wide of the mark when he attacks in this Way commissioners who are not here to defend themselves. I submit that no hon. gentleman should reflect on a member of the public service either directly or indirectly unless he is prepared to go further and make a definite charge.

I think the position taken by the Prime Minister is very fair, and I will be equally fair by withdrawing any implication there may be in my remarks. But I do say to him that I have simply expressed in my statement the point of view that has been expressed to me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I might say
that there is hardly a man in the public service who is not criticized in a similar manner by some opponent.

All that
may be very true; but it would be to the interest of the government, and the commission itself that any suspicion of that kind should not be allowed to continue. My proposal to the Prime Minister would be that in all cases of this kind where any such question arises, where there is any doubt in his mind as to either the commission itself or the recommendations that come from it, the matter should be referred to a committee of this house; and I will in a moment quote the right hon. Prime Minister's own words in that regard. I stated a little earlier that other countries had found it quite practicable to place under the operation of the merit system and to make subject to examination appointments of men, such as ordinary day labourers, much less higher positions. Let me quote a memorandum which I have in my hand respecting some of the regulations covering the appointment of unclassified labourers in the federal service of the United States. This is an extract from regulations of the United States Civil Service Commission, published in the report of the commission for the year ending June 30, 1922, Regulation No. 1 provides:
1.	The Civil Service Commission is authorized to apply these regulations to such cities or parts of the executive civil service as it may deem expedient.
2.	It shall be the duty of all officers in the executive civil service to aid the commission in all proper ways in carrying these regulations into effect.
I will pass over the qualifications of applicants and come to the particular subject under discussion, the point of eligibility:

I turn then to the report of William C. Deming, who explained the details and advantages of the merit system. At that time he was head of the federal Civil Service Commission of the United States. Take unskilled labourers, for example:
Those who seek employment as unskilled labourers are given a physical examination only. It would be useless to test a pick-and-shovel man or a charwoman in arithmetic or geography.
I quite agree with him. But when opponents of the merit system state that it is not practical to make an eligible list for unskilled labourers, I say the evidence of what has been done in other countries must disabuse their minds of that point of view.
For the mechanical trades,-
And, by the way, an enormous number of Skilled artisans have been excluded by order in council passed by this government.
-a physical examination is required which constitutes 40 per cent of the total rating. The other 60 per cent is given to a rating on training and experience in the particular trade upon which application is made.
I could go on and quote what they do in all other cases, such as the technical professions, book-keepers, stenographers, file clerks, general clerks, and so on, through the whole rota of possible positions.
We also find, Mr. Speaker, that parliamentary reports from beginning to end since 1877 have consistently denounced patronage in the government service. Let me refer very briefly to these reports. A committee under the chairmanship of Mr. George Casey, M.P., reported in April, 1877, and this is an extract from the report:
Political patronage is responsible for other evils, and we do not hesitate to express the conviction that many unnecessary civil offices have been retained, and that new places have been created, for no better purpose than to provide for the followers of influential politicians.
Again,
Generally speaking, political influence has been found to interfere more or less in the working of all branches of the service, and always with bad effect.
IMr. E. J. Garland.]
'*'And always with bad effect." Here is another extract from the first report of a commission to investigate the civil service, of which Mr. Donald Mclnnes, of Hamilton, was chairman, and Mr. Martin J. Griffin, secretary. This was on March 5, 1881. The report says:
It-
The patronage system.
-embarrasses ministers in providing an efficient public service, and it causes great and often irresistible pressure to be brought on members of parliament to force their consent to the nomination and appointment of unfit persons.
That last statement, Mr. Speaker, I wish to repeat.
-and, it causes great and often irresistible pressure to be brought on members of parliament to force their consent to the nomination and appointment of unfit persons.
Now the question has been put to me: Am I not in a better position to nominate a postmaster for a little village in my riding than the Civil Service Commission? My answer is twofold. First, I do not know- although I probably could learn-the qualifications required to fill the position. That, however, could be overcome, and possibly I should be as well able as the commission to determine from a stated form the eligibility of any individual who might apply or whom I might have in mind for nomination. But the statement of this commission has the strongest force in matters of the kind, that the member himself does not always feel free-although he may be independent enough to act freely-in making the appointments if he has it in his power to do so. The pressure1 of political partyism is too strong upon him, the need for getting his friends into office is frequently too apparent to him, and there is the inclination on his part that is almost inescapable to appoint, other things not even being equal, those who are his political friends. I ask any hon. member opposite to place himself in a position where two men are applying for a postmastership; one of them is a frank and avowed Conservative, a man who does not agree with the hon. gentleman politically at all; the other is a good friend of his own political persuasion. Now, this good friend of his own political persuasion may not be quite as efficient as the other applicant, but it is very easy to argue-
'Some hon. MEMBERS: Why not?

He may not be in this particular case. It is very easy for +be hon. gentleman who has the appoint-

Civil Service Act-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
ment in his hands to say to himself: Oh, well, the other chap is a good friend of mine;
I am sure he' will be all right anyhow; I will let the thing go through; I don't want to have a Tory in that job anyhow. That is how we are tempted to act; it is human nature. But in the administration of our public service such temptations should be eliminated as far as possible. Let me quote an extract from a report of a commission composed of Messrs. J. M. Courtney, chairman. Thomas Fyshe and P. J. Bazin, on March 17, 1903:
That entrance to and promotions in the service should not he a matter of political patronage, but that the whole outside service should be placed under the Civil Service Commission: that promotion therein should be by merit, and that the higher positions should be filled from the service itself.
A commission composed of G. N. Ducharme and R. S. Lake reported to much the same effect on November 9, 1912. In the report of Commissioners Slack, Lewis and Eugene Tarte in 1918 we find much the same language; in fact, the language of this report was even more trenchant. The statement appears:
General conditions in the printing bureau may be briefly described as shocking. They are. however, the perfectly natural consequence of the "system" which created them. Under any but government ownership the sheriff would long ago have closed the doors of the plant.
Much the same language is used in the report submitted in 1921 by the parliamentary committee of which Mr. Spinney was chairman. and in the final report of the special parliamentary committee brought down in June 1923 under the chairmanship of Mr. James Malcolm we find1:
Your committee is of the opinion that the two fundamental principles of the Civil Service Act are the merit system and the system of appointment by competitive examination, and that both these principles must be preserved.
They did not say "in part"; they did not say that the principle must be preserved with respect to the service generally but not as regards 13,000 positions. The statement is explicit that, in the opinion of the committee, the merit system should be faithfully adhered to. Let me now give an extract from a report of a special committee of the Senate, session 1924, under the chairmanship of the Hon. F. L. Beique:
Your committee is convinced that the method of appointment and promotion by competition (usually known as the merit system), is preferable, in every way, to advancement by favour or influence. In support of this principle may be cited the
findings of a number of committees, extracts from which will be found in the appendix to this report.
I have already' quoted from some of these findings. My time is going and although there is much that I should like to say I must curtail my remarks. The ideal condition in government would be one in which the administrative function, in so far as it is generally applicable, would be separated from the political function. The political function in the business of government is the function responsible for policy and authority. I am speaking in broad terms. I admit there may be modifications of that rule from time to time, and in certain instances but broadly speaking the political function is one of policy and authority. The administrative function, the civil service, has for its duty the carrying out in a business like manner of the policy determined by the political. To do this properly the administrative should not be hampered by the political nor vice versa.
I hesitate at this stage to bring to the attention of the house the record of the Liberal party in this connection. It is not one of which I am proud personally, because I adhere to the merit principle and believe in it, and because the Liberal party, through its greatest leaders, has from time to time expressed itself in determined tones on this question, and now to find them in office under pressure from their friends, from the commission, or from some other source going back upon their own stated principles and repudiating their own convictions is to me repugnant. I am not going to weary the house with a recitation of all the orders in council. Let it suffice to say that the positions which are to-day exempt from the Civil Service Act number between thirteen and fourteen thousand, roughly, and this in spite of the words of the Prime Minister himself. The right hon. gentleman, speaking in Ottawa on September 11, 1926, is reported to have said:
May I say further, ladies and gentlemen, that I stand strongly, and have always stood, for the merit system and promotion on the basis of merit and will do my utmost to see that that is maintained. I might say much more, but being in the middle of an election and on the eve of the day of polling, I naturally have to be somewhat reserved and careful in the statements that I make.
Now that the election is over may I cordially invite the Prime Minister to abandon that reserve and carefulness and regale the house with exactly what he would like to have told that meeting in Ottawa. He continued:
I do not wish to say anything here that is other than in accord with what were our

Mr. Speaker, I endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Maisonneuve

He was referring to the Union, government, and now I apply his own words to himself: I say that this government is not giving proper support to the Civil Service Commission. I must now pass on. Charles Murphy was one of the most brilliant exponents of the merit principle and he exploited, it on every occasion to condemn patronage.
May I ask a question?

I have only forty minutes. The hon. gentleman will make a speech himself, I have no doubt. So far as this question is concerned, I must say that in my seven years in this house I have found no more honest, convincing and consistent supporter of the merit principle than the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, and I appeal to hon. gentlemen on my right to follow the leadership of that man in this matter. I feel that their present leader will follow in his footsteps; I hope he will adhere to the merit principle as the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen did. Let me quote Mr. Meighen's statement:
We put the civil service on the rock basis of merit, although this was done in the face of the bitterest of party opposition, but the task was achieved. I want to say that under any government of which I shall be the head the civil service will continue to stand on the rock basis of the merit system.

A burst of applause followed that pronouncement of policy. Mr. Meighen went on to say that the civil service was in danger and he mentioned certain matters of a partisan character to which I need not refer. He also referred to a statement made by the Minister of National Defence, " now sometimes called minister of self defence," the Hon. E. M. Macdonald of Pictou, to the following effect:
Of all the facts of which Mr. Meighen is guilty, the one unforgivable sin I can never forget is the passing of the Civil Service Act . . . . There lies the greatest danger that surrounds the civil service, and keep this in mind, in so far as you vote.
I ask you too to keep that in mind when voting now. We find also that His Honour the Speaker, before his elevation to that office, is reported as follows-Hansard, May 2, 1921:
In Canada, my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster), who is the senior member of this house, knows how the lives of ministers of the crown have been made unhappy through this infernal patronage system	 Is there a member of this parliament with any selfrespect who of his own free will would return to the days when lobbies were filled with office seekers who made parliamentary life almost unbearable by their importunate demands?

speechtext:
I want the
house to hear the orders in council. I have no objection to my hon. friend reading them if the house will give him permission, but I would ask him whether he has not reference to the orders in council passed under the following clause of the ' Civil Service Act:
In any case where the commission decides that it is not practicable nor in the public interest to apply this act to any position or positions, the commission may, with the approval of the governor in council, exclude such position or positions in whole or in part from the operations of the act, and make such regulations as are deemed advisable prescribing how such position or positions are to be dealt with.
That is the clause in the act under which the orders in council referred to by my hon. friend were passed. One of the classes exempted under that provision is all positions where the salary does not exceed 8200 per annum. I have no doubt that if my hon. friend includes in his figures all those persons whose salaries have been under 8200 per annum he may be quite correct in the numbers he gives, but it is very misleading to represent that the government have taken from under the control of the Civil Service Commission by order in council thousands of positions, when these orders in council have been passed as being in the public interest, and in fact at the instance of the Civil Service Commission itself.
Mr. E R. E. CHEVRIER (Ottawa): Mr. Speaker, I have made my position so clear upon a number of similar occasions that I need not take very much of the time of the house to-day. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) has stated that since this government came into power they have released 14,000 positions from the control of the Civil Service Commission. The facts do not warrant that statement. If we consult the journals of the house for 1923 we find that Dr. Roche, in giving evidence before the parliamentary committee, stated that there were orders in council passed by the previous administration, particularly that order in council passed in September, 1921, which exempted over 11,000 positions and by the word "positions" I mean categories under which people had been employed. On June 29, 1922, when this government were in power, order in council No. 1053 was passed, which recited all the orders in council which had been passed by the previous administration having to do with these exemptions. Dr. Roche stated that up to that time about 13,000 positions had been released, and that the order in council of June 29, 1922, released only 3,000, so my hon. friend was quite in error when he stated that this administration had exempted 14,000 positions.
Then the hon. gentleman quoted a sentence from the Malcolm report, which stated that the merit system must be preserved at all costs.	That is nothing	new to me;	I	wasone of	those who wrote	that sentence	in	thereport,	and ever since	then, in my	everyutterance and in every way I have bound myself	to support the	merit system.	But
there are two kinds of merit systems. It is far from my thoughts that we should destroy the Civil Service Commission altogether; there must be some kind of a commission. There was such a commission in 1908; it was improved from time to time, and we might as well be frank about it. The Civil Service Commission is not a sort of old King Tut's grave, upon which we must not place an unholy hand; we must be able to speak about that commission without being charged with the desire to destroy it. Surely the Civil Service Act is not above reproach, like Caesar's wife, and surely one can say something about it in an honest effort to improve it without being charged with having a nefarious or murderous intent. If we had a little more co-operation; if the hon. gentlemen who speak in such glowing terms about the merit system would only view these problems as we have to view them, we might get somewhere. In 1918 the Civil Service Act was amended for the purpose of allowing the Griffenhagen classification to be adopted into the service. That was one of the most unnatural classifications ever made, and the service feels its effect even to-day. It will be years and years before the noxious seeds of that classification are completely eradicated from the civil service, and those who suffer most are the civil servants themselves. The Civil Service Commission did wonderful work in trying to solve the difficulty, but this classification was introduced at that time and the Civil Service Commission was reorganized. That law was framed in haste, and it was drawn up for a purpose which had nothing do with the Civil Service Commission.
Civil Service Act-Mr. Chevrier

Surely it will be admitted that that law, as is the ease with every law, was not perfect in the beginning; surely certain features may be improved from time to time.
When I mention co-operation between the government and the civil servants I come immediately to what has been advocated for some years, a closer bond between these different elements which will probably come about through the medium of civil service councils. I quite agree that the merit system must be preserved and that all entrants into the civil service should pass a competitive examination. We are told now that the civil service law of Canada is designed exactly along the lines of the laws prevailing in other countries, but we have not been told as yet the names of those countries. If my hon. friend refers to the English civil service law he refers to something which does not exist, because there is no civil service law in England. In that country there is only a series of orders in council, which give the greatest latitude to the heads of the different departments. I hold in my hand photostat copies of those orders in councils, if anyone would care to see them. Then my hon. friend said there was a civil service law in the United States; he referred particularly to the state of New Jersey, and stated that everyone was admitted to the civil service of that state through the merit system and a competitive examination. Then I find at page 30 that in the state of New Jersey there is a noncompetitive class and this is what is said with respect to it:
Positions in the non-competitive class shall be those of a minor character, the filling of which is impracticable either through competitive examination or through registration under the provisions of rule XI.
There is another provision about the noncompetitive class in the state of New York. At page 10 we find the following:
In the state service, all unskilled labourers and such skilled labourers as are not included in the competitive class or the non-competitive class; and in addition thereto there may be included in the exempt class all other subordinate offices for the filling of which competitive or non-competitive examination may be found to be not practicable. But no office or position shall be deemed to be in the exempt class unless it is specifically named in such class in the rules, and the reasons for each such exemption shall be stated separately in the annual reports of the commission. Not more than one appointment shall be made to or under the title of any such office or position, unless a different number is specifically mentioned in such rules. Appointments to positions in the exempt class may be made without examination.
The same words that are used in the Canadian law.
fMr. Chevrier.]
Now as to the differences between the Canadian Civil Service Act and the British Civil Service Act, let me say this: I have quoted this memorandum time and again, and it no doubt appears in Hansard. I have often quoted it on public platforms. This is what it says:
The head of a Canadian department who is responsible for the carrying out of the work of that department is told by the commission what clerical assistance he will require and is then furnished with that assistance, and he is further told by the commission what professional and technical assistance he will require and is furnished with such persons to do that technical and professional work as the commission decide have the qualifications. If the head of the department wants more help, he notifies the commission who decide whether he does or not and what kind of help is needed.
The British commission is subject to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, and is not independent of parliament as is the Canadian. It makes all appointments (after examination, approved by the treasury) unless the position is wholly or partially professional or has requirements otherwise peculiar and not ordinarily to be acquired in the civil service in which cases the head of the department nominates the appointee. Also in cases where the head of the department and the treasury consider it to be in the public interest, they may dispense with all or part of the qualifications-
And so on. I am not blaming the Civil Service Commission for administering the law as they find it. I have pointed out the defects of that law but I cannot blame them for administering the law as they find it. I should like to see the responsibility placed where it should lie, namely, with certain provisions and certain qualifications, upon the deputy head or the minister himself.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that it is a great privilege indeed to have such a fine protective staff as we have in connection with this Hous.e of Commons, the finest body of men I believe that ever occupied positions in this building. Now if parliament had not the privilege of choosing these men or having the final say, do you think we should have such a fine and well disciplined body of men as we have now? The responsibility for looking after this body of men is placed upon the Sergeant-at-Arms who acts under the direction of Mr. Speaker. I for one am satisfied that if the Civil Service Commission had to choose the members of this staff it would not be as fine a body of men as it is to day nor would the discipline be as good. It stands to reason that that could not be otherwise.	.

Does not the responsibility for the appointment of these men rest upon parliament itself, or one who represents parliament, namely, Mr. Speaker?

Civil Service Act-Mr. Campbell

Indirectly the staff are
under the control of parliament but Mr. Speaker and his officers are immediately in control. There is a directing hand. Somebody assumes responsibility for the appointments and the personal element and the personal touch are noticeable. It could not be done in any other way. Except where otherwise expressly provided, all appointments to the civil service shall be upon competitive examination-

It is discharging a duty which has been imposed upon it and it is honestly discharging that duty. Now a moment ago I referred to order in council No. 1053. The civil service commissioners are of opinion that the following classes of positions should be exempt from the operation of the Civil Service Act under the above section-

Upon one occasion I had a man appointed as postmaster of a $60 a year post office. Does not my hon. friend from Mackenzie think I had reason to ask for the dismissal of that man? There were not very many dismissals in my constituency, but those few were made for good reasons. Another postmaster kept a letter addressed to his brother-in-law, who lived in front of his house, for over a month. That letter contained a cheque for $125; the postmaster knew it belonged to his brother-in-law, but

because of some family trouble the letter was not delivered for one month. The postmaster offered the letter to people of the same name when he knew it was intended for his brother-in-law, and in addition to that the postmaster was very well known as a drunkard. I think in this case my hon. friend from Mackenzie would have done as I did. I have quoted only three cases in my constituency; we have 245 constituencies in this country, and if we multiply that number by three we have twice the number of dismissals made by the Postmaster General, so I think I am very reasonable in that calculation.
I believe this matter should be considered in a broad way.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to see I am
beginning to convince my hon. friend from Mackenzie. The hon. member for Bow River is one of the cleverest members of this house, and I am sorry he is not in his seat at present. I wanted to ask him a question during his speech, but he refused to let me ask it. I would be more generous, and would give him ample time now to answer the question. Aa matters stand at present, are all important appointments with the exception of those mentioned in this bill made by the Civil Service Commission? We all know that that is not so. You know very well, Mr. Speaker, that every deputy minister is appointed by the governor in council, and that judges, whose dignity is above suspicion, are also appointed by the governor in council. You know very well that senators, those dignified old gentlemen, to which body I am glad to see some younger men have been appointed, are named by the governor in council, and you also know that ambassadors, charges d'affaires and ministers are appointed in the same way. When we come to some of the most important appointments in the civil service of this country, we do not go to the Civil Service Commission, We do not ask applicants for the position of Auditor General to pass an examination; the Auditor General is appointed by a vote of this house, and that also applies to the Chief Electoral Officer. Those are two of the most important positions in Canada. I am acquainted with most of the deputy ministers, whom I admire very much for their experience, their sense of duty and their responsibilities as public officials. There is only one exception, whom I will not name to-day, a gentleman who has occupied his position for quite a long time and who is known to hold a private correspondence with a former minister. That deputy suffers now from neurasthenia, and perhaps some time later I will

Civil Service Act-Mr. Pouliot
bring his case before this house. As an example, however, let us consider Mr. Hunter, the Deputy Minister of Public Works. He has a huge responsibility, as assistant to the head of one of the most important departments of governments, and he is a most capable man. Take the chief engineer, Mr. Cameron. He has just been elected president of the graduates of McGill university. He is well known in this country, is a very capable man, and his staff is composed of highly qualified officials. I wish to say something also about the divisional engineers whom I know, and who are very competent men, for instance, Mr. Sabourin, of Quebec, Mr. Bertrand, and Mr. Amyot, of Rimouski. I know these gentlemen well. They are very good men, and I do not think one of them was appointed by the Civil Service Commission as constituted to-day. They were appointed before the commission had such powers as were given to it by the late lamented leader ol the opposition, personally a most charming man. He was then I think Solicitor General or Minister of the Interior.
I have just been speaking of the Public Works department. Now let us take the department of the Postmaster General, whom I see here. The minister is a very competent man. Mr. Gaboury is a most excellent deputy minister; everyone will admit that. Mr. Coolican, assistant deputy minister, is a first-class officer. Mr. Anderson, superintendent of the mail service, is a friend of every man in this house. Mr. Gagnon is a young officer but very well qualified; and so on. Most of these officials were appointed outside of the Civil Service Commission. Take the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). He too has reason to be proud of his staff. The deputy minister, Dr. Grisdale, comes from Quebec, and is known as a very competent man. Dr. Charron, his assistant, is a chemist and possesses bilingual qualifications. His name is well known and respected in Quebec.
Throughout Canada too.

Yes, throughout Canada
too. I mentioned Quebec because Dr. Charron has lived in that province for a long time. Take Mr. Archibald, director of experimental farms; he is a gentleman of worldwide renown, and all the heads of branches in that department are very competent men. Most of them were appointed before the Civil Service Commission commenced to make appointments.
Take the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning). He has a very good deputy minister. We do not get much from that department
because the railways are now in the Canadian National system. But I wish to praise the officers of the Department of Railways and Canals also. The chief engineer, Colonel Duhue, is a gentleman distinguished in his profession. I think he was appointed at the request of the minister and the Civil Service Commission had very little to do with the appointment.
In the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment there are some very capable men, especially since the recent changes have been carried out. I am sure that the minister will not discontinue the good work but will persist in the determination to secure the highest efficiency in the department. May I take this opportunity to say that I hope the Board of Pension Commissioners, whose term expires this year, will be allowed to return home. We have had enough of those people. I am here to say what I think about them, and I am very sorry that no investigation was made into the board. After what I heard the other day in the committee room, I do not believe that Mr. Thompson is qualified to act for another term. I hope the next time the minister makes an appointment he will appoint a French Canadian on the board, because the French Canadians have good records as soldiers. If the minister does not choose a French Canadian he should .at least appoint one member who has bilingual qualifications, and who will recognize that when the appeal board gives a judgment it should be respected.
I see the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Forke) here. He is always in good humour, he never experiences any trouble, and he has a very important department. Everyone likes the minister. He has a very good deputy minister in the person of Mr. W. J. Egan, amongst whose accomplishments is a knowledge of the French language. I am sure that within a few years the people of this country will recognize the benefits of the new policy that that department is going to carry out in the best interests of the country. At this stage I wish to ask the Minister of Immigration and Colonization not to forget the very eloquent speech made the other day by my hon. friend the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) on the opportunities to be given-

May I remind the hon.
gentleman that he is discussing matters not relevant to this debate?

I have said what I wanted to say and the Minister of Immigration and Colonization has heard my recommendations. I am sure he will take note of them.

Take the Department of Justice, which is one of the most important departments in this country. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is the first lawyer in Canada. He is a very able man and is greatly respected in this house. He also has good assistants. His former deputy minister is now sitting on the bench of the highest tribunal in Canada. I refer to Mr. Justice Newcombe. Mr. Edwards, his successor, is a very able jurist. His assistant is Mr. Renaud who was a Conservative. He is a very able man and has a command of both the English and French languages. He was appointed when the Conservatives were in power and had they always made such appointments, they would not have been blamed by anybody on the Liberal side. But that was not the case.
Are you willing to introduce a resolution to do away with the Civil Service Commission?

If that is what my hon.
friend advocates, I think he is right in a certain sense and I will explain that later on. I do not say he is altogether right. We have the department of my hon. friend, the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) Whom I see here with his broad smile. Everything goes smoothly in his department, but he has many things to do. He is the head of a department which looks after incorporations of companies and naturalization, and may I say that all requests are not granted and that every request is thoroughly investigated before any action is taken. The Secretary of State has a very able assistant in the person of his deputy minister, Mr. Mulvey, who is a well-known author on company law and whose book is very often quoted before the courts. He also has as his chief legal adviser, Mr. O'Meara, who is one of the best lawyers in Canada.
I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in his seat and I wish to pay a special compliment to him because, in a very popular ministry, I think he is the most popular, especially amongst business men. He is working very hard for the people of this country, but he has some very capable assistants who help him in reducing taxes, in reducing the national debt and in rendering service to the people. I am not going to speak of all the departments, but if we consider the amount of work that is done by every civil servant in Canada we are bound to give them our greatest admiration.
The Department of the Interior at Ottawa is an immense department. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) has a very good deputy minister, but he has also in his de-

partment quite a number of specialists, men who are very capable and who would perhaps command from three to five times as much in the way of salary if they were working for private concerns instead of being public servants. May I mention three gentlemen whom I know very well, namely, Mr. F. C. C. Lynch, director of natural resources intelligence service, and his assistants, Mr. Sherrin and Mr. Chalifour, men whose high capabilities are most valuable to the service in which they are engaged.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I do not see the relevancy of his remarks to the subject under discussion. I do not know if he intends to apply his remarks to the objects of the bill now before the house.

I have been speaking for a few minutes but I will explain why I make these remarks. The object of this bill is to bring the appointment of all public servants under the Civil Service Commission and I have been instancing some civil servants whose rank is very important, whose capacities are great, but whose appointments have nothing to do with the Civil Service Commission. I trust that explanation will suffice to allow me to continue with what I have to say.

The hon.
member should complete the record of the departments. He has covered them all except the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the Solicitor-General and the Secretary of State.

I was included and I
was honoured by being so included.
I am keeping the Department of Marine and Fisheries for the last, but I wish to say something about my genial friend, the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon).
Say it with lilies.

Yes, I will say it with
lilies, and I will bring them to the Solicitor General whose capacity is great and whose heart is open to understand the misfortunes of life. He is always ready to give full consideration to every case that is brought to his attention. He is helped in that connection by a very clever lawyer, Mr. Gallagher, chief of the remission branch, who was appointed by the Conservatives, who was the legal partner of Mr. Patenaude in Montreal, but might I say that he was the sun while Mr. Patenaude was the moon? Mr. Gallagher is a very clever lawyer; his sense of duty is great, and when a case is

Civil Service Act-Mr. Pouliot
submitted to him he takes care to read the whole file and to act conscientiously. I do not believe he was appointed by the Civil Service Commission. He was not appointed by our party but his selection was a very good move on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite. This is another instance, and if they had always made such appointments, no one would blame them for their appointments.

The hon. member has
named quite a number of good ones they made.

I named a couple of good ones and I may name some more. To complete what I have to say about the Solicitor General may I add that he is acknowledged by all as the best lawyer of his generation, not only in Quebec but in Canada at large?
In the world.

Not in the world. That would be over-stating the case. When the Solicitor General is ten years older we shall say he is the greatest lawyer in the world.
I will say that he is the best lawyer of his generation in this country.
Turning to the Department of Marine and Pisheries, we have as minister the most eloquent French Canadian, indeed the most eloquent speaker that I have ever heard in my life.

I would ask the hon.
gentleman to speak to the bill.

I am through with what
I had to say, Mr. Speaker, in regard to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin). I come now to his deputy minister, of whom I spoke at the beginning of my remarks. I think it is a shame for any civil servant to be disloyal to his minister, and the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries has been disloyal to his minister.
OrdeT. It is not permissible to attack in that way a permanent official who is not in the house.

I will take up this case
when the estimates of the Department of Marine and Fisheries come up, and I will remember his letter about the port of Montreal. In that department there are very capable men, such as Mr. Rodd, who is the head of the fish culture branch, and1 another gentleman, Mr. Cowie, a specialist, who I think was not appointed by the Civil Service Commission. He is a remarkable man.
Now may I continue my argument? There are other brilliant men whose names I could
not enumerate in the short time at my disposal, who deserve the consideration of this country because of their high qualifications, their great experience and profound knowledge, and their good service to the state. Some of them have been appointed by the Conservative party, others have been appointed by the Liberal party, but when a man does his duty we do not need to ask by whom he was appointed. All we ask is that he fulfil his duty according to his conscience, and according to what is expected of him. That is the way I look at it, Mr. Speaker. When I approach a civil servant for any information,
I do not inquire whether he was appointed by the Conservatives or the Liberals. I inquire, first of all, whether he is a conscientious man who does his duty .
Then he must be a Liberal; he cannot be anything else.

Perhaps he is not a Liberal in politics, but he should have a liberal mind. When a man is appointed to the public service, whether by the Civil Service Commission or by the governor in council, he should the moment he is appointed forget the party to which he belonged and become independent. Instead of wasting his time in small matters of politics, he should attend to the duties of his office, and devote himself to the service of his country. That is the way I look at it, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure that no member of this house will disagree with that point of view. If a former minister whose name is not forgotten in this house has been betrayed by people in his department who did not have that sense of duty, he was betrayed by people who were appointed by the Civil Service Commission.
I listened with attention to what my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) had to say regarding his bill, and I heard him make a philosophical mistake. His phraseology was rather strange. He made an affirmation; he said that this government was not giving proper support to the Civil Service Commission. I rose for the purpose of asking what he meant by those words, but I did not 'have the opportunity to put my question. I would ask him now if he thinks the government is not giving proper support to the Civil Service Commission because of the fact that there are still some positions which are not under the control of the commission. The philosophical mistake that my hon. friend made was this. He took as a fact that the Civil Service Commission is an infallible body, that it cannot make mistakes. I have nothing to say against the Civil Service Commissioners; I respect them; I think they are good men; but they

Civil Service Act-Mr. Manion
can make mistakes. Here in this house we have 245 members, a member from every corner of this country, and no one is supposed to know the people of his county better than their representative in this house. Moreover, each member is interested in making reliable recommendations to any member of the government. If I recommend a man in my county who is not qualified for a particular position, T shall be the first one to suffer, because people will blame me for my recommendation. But if a member takes the responsibility of recommending for any government position the best man available, he has the satisfaction of having done his duty.
Time.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up very much time of the house naturally, after the very excellent and eloquent address of the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Pouliot), there is not very much more to be said on the subject. I am sorry for this, not on my own account, but because I know my hon. leader (Mr. Bennett), my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and one or two other hon. gentlemen did intend to take part in this debate.
I am very sorry.

I notice the regret evinced by the hon. gentleman. I rise, Mr. Speaker, to support in a general way the measure of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). I do so with some qualifications, because since coming into this house eleven years ago I must admit that it is not always possible to live up to the ideals of our earlier years; we find that the real and the ideal do not always jibe. It is true that public opinion is largely in favour of the so-called merit system; that is, the system under which the Civil Service Commission makes all the appointments to the government service. Since public opinion should rule in a democratic country, that system should prevail, particularly as we have a Civil Service Commission which is supposed to make all such appointments. This being so, I d'o agree with the hon. member for Boiw River that it would be better either to give the Civil Service Commission power to make all these appointments, or throw the commission aside altogether and get back to the old patronage system. Let us have at least straightforwardness and honesty in this matter. If we are to go back to the old system, let us do so frankly and openly instead of following the insidious practice of the government.
The reason that I am giving the bill a more or less qualified support is that over a 
period of years before I became a member of this house I saw many appointments made under the old patronage system by both parties, just as the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) has said, and most of them were excellent appointments. I say that quite frankly. I have also seen appointments made since by both parties, and those too for the most part have been excellent appointments. In fact a large proportion of the appointments made by both parties in the past have been of an excellent character because1, generally speaking, they were made on the responsibility of the member concerned, who, of course, had to answer to his constituents for what he had done.
Now, sir, in regard to the so-called savings that may be made under a civil service commission as opposed to the cost under the old patronage system, I submit that under neither system can we be expected to live up to the economic standards of private corporations. There is a public charity which must be taken into account to a certain extent, and I think it would be regrettable if under either the merit or the patronage system we hewed absolutely to the line, sternly refusing on all occasions to give a position to anybody unless he fully deserved it and was fitted for it, because there are times when for the good of the country it is far better to give a man a position than to throw him out on the rather cold charity of the world.
The Union Government of which I was a supporter did, in 1918, put under the Civil Service Commission of that day practically all appointments both in the inside and the outside service. Since then thousands of positions have been taken out of the hands of the commission. And I am a little surprised at my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Chev-rier) supporting the system whereby he and his confrere have to make so many recommendations on behalf of applicants for certain positions. On many occasions I have talked the matter over with other hon. members who then represented the Ottawa district, men just as upright as the hon. gentleman himself, but invariably they told me they were happier to see all the appointments made by the Civil Service Commission, because under the old conditions they were practically pestered to death by applicants for patronage.
I know my hon. friend from Ottawa who-spoke this afternoon is in exactly the same position to-day. Pass along the hall where his room is situated and at any time of the day you will find people chasing him for positions on the Rfdeau canal.
In spite of some criticisms to the contrary at times, I believe the Civil Service Com-

Civil Service Act-Mr. Manion
mission, as constituted, has done excellent work. I have had many dealings with it in a more or less formal way, as all members have, and while I do not know that I ever received a favour from it, I believe its decisions for the most part have been just, fair and reasonable. Because of that, Mr. Speaker, I think the government ought to accept this bill and make it an absolute rule to go back to the system of appointment to the civil service by the commission. Undoubtedly the merit system is supported by public opinion. I have given reasons why I am not so enthusiastic about it as are some other members. I have been longer in the house than my hon. friend from Bow River, I know he is absolutely sincere in his attitude in regard to this matter, as are many others, particularly the newer members, but I do not think they have1 had as wide an experience as I have had; and I repeat, to my mind it would be entirely safe to go back to the old system provided it was not abused. It was not the old spoils or .patronage system which was wrong, it was the abuse of the system. But, as I have said before, having the merit system in vogue to-day, we should support it to the fullest extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I may ask my hon. friend a question. The staff of the Soldier Settlement Board and the Income Tax Board were appointed under the administration of which he was a supporter. Does he say now that those appointments were in any way inferior to the apointments made by the Civil Service Commission?

No. If my hon. friend had been listening to me he would have observed that I have taken the attitude that most of the appointments .made by both parties ini the past have been reasonably good appointments. In the pamphlet which the Minster of Finance sent across here a few minutes ago, it is said there are experts in the different departments whom it would be better to have chosen by the officers of those departments. That may be true. Still I adhere to the position that it is the desire largely of the people that the Civil Service Commission should have jursdiction. That is the desire also in England, apparently, and it is becoming Largely the desire in. the United States. In view of this I believe that we should continue our system of appointment under the Civil Service Commission.
Before six o'clock is called, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word to the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot). When the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) was speaking, the Postmaster General pointed out that many of
the 421 dismissals made by his department, and claimed by the hon. member as political patronage dismissals, were made because of theft, drunkenness, incompetence and other crimes or irregularities. I have no intention of arguing the matter with the Postmaster General, but I submit to him in all sincerity that he owes it in justice to the other postmasters in various parts of the country, who were dismissed on grounds of political patronage, to give, at the earliest opportunity, a list of those who were dismissed for that particular reason, together with a list of those who were dismissed on any other account.
The returns have been on the table for the last two weeks.

But they are not accessible to the people. When the minister made the statement, inadvertently I think, that a large proportion had been dismissed because of drunkenness, stealing, incompetence and other offences of that kind, he did not tell us how many there were. He did not say what the proportion was.
It is in the return.

Yes, but the return is not accessible to the people, and unless the Postmaster General makes it perfectly clear who were dismissed cn these charges it is a reflection on the whole 421 who were dismissed. It is unjust to them.
I do not intend to be unjust, and when my estimates are under consideration I will dissect all dismissals and give full information to the house.

That is what I was suggesting. I am quite sure the minister does not wish to reflect on the whole 421. I venture to say that a very small percentage will be found to have been dismissed for any such cause as has been stated. Mr. Speaker, may I ask that you call it six o'clock.

Customs tariff-549. Wool, the hair of the camel, alpaca, goat or other like animal, not further prepared than combed: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):

I think I explained the other day that the importation under these other items was very small.

This is another case
where we do not seem to be doing anything, because nothing at all came in under old item 555 during 1926, and in fact nothing has come in under that item since 1923. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I would ask the minister if he knows whether or not any ruling was made by a customs board or any other body which enabled wool which had previously come in under item 555 to come in free under item 554?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that has been the
practice for a good many years.

What is the reason for that? It looks like sharp practice on someone's part to make a separate item under which sheep's wool is dutiable, and then to allow it in free under another item. This is the kind of thing whi-ch makes me think there will be grave difficulty in the future in connection with the different classes of rags which come in free and the others which come in under a duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think from the time this item was first placed in the tariff many years ago a ruling was made that it was of a class not produced in Canada.

I would like to ask the Minister of Finance why the duty is lowered on wool and kept at its former level on the

finshed article? Is it possible that the manufacturers of wool were not able to pay dividends, or have not secured the profits they wished to secure, or did the tariff advisory board give any advice at all in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I explained that to my hon. friend a few days ago. In this reclassification we are getting rid of two items which are practically obsolete. My hon. friend from Peace River just pointed out that there were practically no imports under those items.

I would like to make just one final appeal to the minister. My personal opinion of the Minister of Finance is so high that I find it very difficult to criticize his estimates, but I do feel that he is doing an injury to the people whom I have the honour to represent and to the people of the country generally when he takes away the little protection at present enjoyed by the farmers of Canada. We know the destructive effect this Australian treaty has had upon the dairying industry, and I would like to make a last appeal to the minister to leave the farmer what little protection he has on his wool. I know the minister is a protectionist, as I think the great majority of the people of this country are protectionists, and for the life of me I cannot see why that principle should not be carried all around the circle. If we are going to give protection to the manufacturers, as we do and as I think it is proper to do, then it is reasonable to give protection to the farmers of this country as well. It seems to me we are discriminating unfairly against a class of people who are doing an enormous amount of work in building up this country, and who get very little consideration. I am quite willing to confess that even when my own party was in power I advocated raising the duty on dairy products and other articles, and I advocate that today. As a protectionist country-and I think that is the established policy of all parties in Canada-we should be fair and carry this protection to all classes. Give it to the manufacturer where it is required; give it to the labouring man by protecting his job, and give it to the farmer as well. I must say that I have a great deal of sympathy with the Finance minister who is buttressed on one side by the tariff board-and if he will take my advice he will scrap that board-and on the other side by our free trade friends from the west who sit immediately to his right. But after all he has a duty to perform to the people of this country, and I should like to make one final appeal to him not to abolish the little protection the farmers of Canada have.

speechtext: Yes.

And we take away a

I should like to join with the hon. gentleman who has just spoken in making an appeal on behalf of the sheep farmers of Canada. It is a very striking feature that while our flocks have not been protected as far as the important wool crop is concerned for very many years in this country, our sheep population has increased only about
100.000	head in 57 years. Certainly we cannot boast about our progress in the sheep line. Our sheep population in Canada is only about
3,000,000 head as compared with something over 90,000,000 in Australia, 27,000,000 in little New Zealand, 23,000,000 in Great Britain, and
44.500.000	in the United States. Another striking feature has been that the United States, where the wool has been protected since 1816, has made steady progress in her sheep development. Perhaps anticipating the war they removed the duty from wool in 1913. The country became filled up with wool, and at the termination of the war the sheep business was in a very depressed condition. So they applied the tariff again. In the United States they have increased their sheep population by about 6.5 per cent within the last twelve months, and in recent months they have had more sheep available for slaughter than they have had since 1914. Comparing the two countries, we have the country upon the one hand where the sheep business has been stabilized by the protection of wool, and on the other hand a situation in Canada where we have been absolutely without protection as far back as I can remember, in the case of wool. On the one hand there has been rapid and substantial progress, and on the other hand very little progress, if indeed any at all. The United States is not considered a great mutton and lamb consuming country. They consume there about 5.4 pounds of mutton and lamb per capita, while in Canada we consume just about 9 pounds, and Great Britain consumes from 50 to 60 pounds. It is a well known fact-it is apparent to every man who is interested in agriculture-that we have huge areas of land
well adapted for the production of sheep and we have only a sheep population of about
3,000,000 head scattered over this vast domain. Our opportunities for the growing of sheep here are immense. They do very well on our ranges; they do as well here as they do anywhere on the continent. Our average clip on the ranges under ordinary conditions would be from 7 to 8 pounds of wool; and in British Columbia in some special flocks, particularly where there is a good Scotchman in charge of the flock, it runs as high as 10 pounds per head. The lamb crop is an excellent one too.
I know of one man in British Columbia who sold 3,000 lambs in September weighing round 80 pounds per head, bringing in a revenue of $30,000, averaging around $10 per head.
I feel that some effort should be made- I am not talking in any critical way because I think, perhaps, the Conservative government has erred just as much as the Liberal government is continuing to err by failing to give some protection to the wool producers-to improve the existing conditions. As far as the production of finer wools is concerned there is no reason why our wool here could not be very much improved, and I am very glad indeed to note that the research council is now taking this matter up. It is well known that we have a long dry belt extending through the length of British Columbia clear down the continent, including such states as Wyoming, Idaho, eastern Washington, and some others, and in those states they are producing fine wools of very excellent quality. As an indication of how good these fine wool sheep are, let me say that at the Salt Lake ram sale, which is held annually, they sold sheep at as high a figure as two and three thousand dollars a head, and within the last few years representatives of the Russian government have come over and purchased very heavily. They had the whole world to select from and they gave the preference to the Salt Lake sale and to other western states, indicating the very marked progress that ;s being made in the breeding of these fine wool sheep. If these sheep can be bred and produced on the American side there is no reason why the same thing cannot be done on the Canadian side where the conditions are very similar.
There has been some complaint about black hair found among the wool of some of our range sheep in the west. I think that is simply a matter of breeding, and by good care that can be overcome. That black hair in the wool is probably due to the fact that without protection for our wool the breeder of sheep aims to rely on his lamb crop rather than on his wool crop, and to produce sheep

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
that will yield both wool and lamb. We might place a reasonable tariff on wool. Perhaps that is not the remedy but I certainly think the situation is serious enough to have a thorough investigation made, and a careful survey of our opportunities, a careful survey of the whole sheep and wool situation. Then 1 think we would soon come to some reasonable conclusion whereby we would place the sheep industry in Canada on a good, sound, sane basis. Our opportunities for development are simply immense along these lines. I call the attention of the government to this particular question hoping they will give it careful consideration and try to develop in this direction.
