The element of protection has very little to do with the diminution in the number of sheep in the United States of America. With them the question is not one of tariff. We are all taught that the United States is a cotton country and the effort of the cotton growers there to displace wool in the clothing of their people produced a fierce conflict which has continued for a great number of years. This point has been brought to our attention in quite a remarkable way in the construction, for instance, of automobiles. In this country the linings of automobiles cost more than in the United States because the latter is a cotton country and they use a great deal of cotton in the upholstery of automobiles, whereas in Canada we use wool entirely.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt
my hon. friend's argument, but he may be able to explain this. Raw cotton, like wool, comes into Canada free of duty.

Just so, but the point we wish to emphasize is simply this. From our geographical situation we have scarcely any other choice of producing the clothing of our people than from our flocks of sheep, and in any country where they are driven to provide their people with clothing from wool you will find the figures very much the reverse of those pointed out by the minister. Such countries have increased the numbers of their flocks and their efforts to produce wool in order to make clothing for their people. Canada is a wool country in general and the United States is to-day a cotton country. That explains those figures much more

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
pointedly and sanely than they can be explained from the point of view of tariff alone.
Our wool problem is not only a matter of tariff. We have for years observed many forces playing upon our people and our farmers in the direction of reducing the flocks of our country. Strange to say, a question that has often come up is that of fencing. Our fencing problem is the same as they have in any other country, and in any country where they claim their flocks are important and where they endeavour in a national way to make their flocks profitable for their people, they overcome the fencing problem. A year or two ago I heard the Minister of Finance raise in this house the question of the dog., It is strange that dogs do not* kill sheep in England, nor in New Zealand, although the dogs and the sheep are of the same type as in this country. Why is that not the case in Canada? In recent years it has been discovered beyond all question that the dog which will undertake to kill sheep has something wrong in his head; he is a crazy dog.
Oh, oh.

All right. In Kentucky they hold trials of dogs. A dog is brought before a magistrate and if it is demonstrated beyond all shadow of doubt that he is the dog that chased or killed a sheep, there is only one penalty and that is death to the dog. In every country where they have eliminated the sheep-killing dog they soon begin to breed dogs that will not kill sheep, and if they have done that in other countries they can do it in Canada.
As the ex-Minister of Agriculture has stated, it is fundamental that the people of this country should inquire into and get at the reasons why our flocks have been reduced. We should regard our flocks as they do in other countries, as one of the finest assets we have and endeavour to increase the numbers. Let us not get it into our heads that the tariff is the only factor. Other factors enter into the question and they should all be considered, an endeavour being made to eliminate all the reasons why our flocks should not be raised up to the numbers or even the percentages they were at the time of confederation. At confederation Canada had more than one sheep per head of poulation and it takes just about one sheep per head of population to supply sufficient wool to clothe the people of a country. Until we get at least one sheep for each head of population we are behind our times and behind our privileges. To me it is amazing to read that in Nova Scotia we have more than a
million acres of land suitable for grazing and yet so few sheep are raised there, although with the wool they could raise they could provide the whole of Canada with the clothing required and be more than ten thousand miles nearer the best market for lamb and mutton than any other sheep-raising country. Yet we see countries away on the other side of the equator coming across the line and capturing a market that is ten or twelve thousand miles away. We can look at this question from a hundred different angles, but they all lead to this point, that we have not lived up to the opportunities that should present themselves to a people such as ours and a country such as this.

I confess that I, a mere professional man, am greatly interested in this wool industry. I have been frequently associated with one of the large business enterprises in western Canada, and it has been my good fortune to have expressed to me from time to time the opinion of one of the pioneer stock men of that country, Mr. P. Burns, regarding the development of our cattle and sheep industry. He has frequently told me that British Columbia, in some parts of it, is better adapted in his opinion to the production of large flocks of sheep than any other part of the country he knows. There are sections of Alberta about which the same might be said. Flocks and herds were the foundations of national wealth in the early days of history, and even until to-day a nation's wealth is measured to some considerable extent by its flocks and herds. This country at the present time has less than three million sheep; it should have not less than nine million if we are to maintain the minimum production of flocks; and having regard to the conditions that obtain here, twenty millions would not be an extravagant number of sheep to be maintained in Canada. But we have only three million, and I think it is fair that we should ask ourselves why we have so small a number. The sheep is a peculiarly profitable animal, because not only is its coat of wool valuable, but the production of mutton and lamb for food purposes may be said to be equally valuable. Under those circumstances this country has made little or no progress with respect to the development of the wool industry, and yet there is no country in the world where woollen clothing is in greater demand or is more of a staple necessity of the people. The people of the west require wool, and with the development of its population we must have large supplies of woollen garments, for without them the people really suffer in the winter. That is so practically all over

There are some eight or ten other mills from which no report could be received by the gentleman whom I asked to get this information. They have only 83 looms, however, and the information that I have given was as full as could be obtained up to that point.
Let it be borne in mind that the first twenty-two mills that I mentioned had all the machinery for preparing, scouring, dyeing, carding, spinning, weaving and finishing wool, and one-half of their capital is invested in plant for manufacturing processes up to yarn. That is an important matter to consider.
I have given this house a list of the woollen mills in Canada. I have shown the condition of the industry on the 21st day of January last, the number of looms idle and the number operating, and in addition, as I said, there are eighty-three looms from which no report was received. Of the number of mills I gave, one-half, practically the first twenty-two mills mentioned, are employed in making use of all processes that convert wool into cloth. They have all the spinning and other machinery that goes with such an industry.
Now what does this tariff propose to do? This tariff, first of all, proposes that machinery shall come in free. I observe that in their submission to the tariff board the French industry strongly urge that French machinery should come in free, and I observe the same with respect to the British industry. That machinery is now to come in free to compete with men who have hundreds of millions of dollars invested in machinery in their industry. It will be a direct incentive to induce people to come in and destroy existing capital in this country. Whatever else may be said by hon. gentlemen opposite, however, strong may be their views with respect to matters of this kind, no less an authority than Adam Smith has pointed out that where you have vested industry established under those circumstances, care should be taken not to destroy the industry. But free machinery is to come in under these tariff proposals.
Then you have free yarns. Who are bene-fitting by this? It means, first of all, that the machinery now engaged in the production of yarns will become idle. You ask, why should that be so? Cannot Canadian industrial enterprise produce yarns quite as cheaply and quite as readily as can the Bradford and other English mills? With respect to that I can only point out that the evidence given to the tariff board, to which I alluded the other day, and from which I should like to read were it
not needlessly taking up the time of the committee, abundantly establishes that under the conditions there obtaining, unless we pay our people a wage on which they cannot live and lower their standard of living to a point that is unendurable, it is impossible for us to compete with them. Who that read the report the other day of the socal service board with respect to child mortality in this country would desire to lower the standard of living in Canada to a level lower than now obtains? I do not think any hon. gentleman would desire to do that. Yet unless we are prepared to do it we must face the fact that placing this yarn upon the free list means that these looms will become idle, and that the capital therein invested will become unproductive and therefore, will be destroyed. I have in my hand the issue of February 22, 1928, of the Textile Argus, published in Bradford. This paper, of course, points out the singular fact to which I alluded the other day.
The changes announced last week by the Canadian Finance minister in tariffs affecting the imports of yarns and fully manufactured goods into Canada would be read with peculiar interest in Bradford. It will be recalled that last year the Canadian manufacturers applied to the tariff board for a revision of import duties which would give them greater protection, and the matter was considered to be of such importance to the trade of Bradford and the West Riding that the West Riding chambers of commerce sent out Mr. J. H. C. Hodgson and the West Riding Manufacturers' Federation, Mr. George H. Wood to place before the tariff board carefully considered reasons why the duties should not be increased. Those who are familiar with the evidence submitted by these two witnesses will realize that they have made an impression on the powers that be in the Dominion, and that their mission to Ottawa last June has been fully justified. There are to be no increased duties on yarns or finished goods. The assistance which the Canadian government is giving to the Canadian manufacturers is to be secured in another and a more acceptable way. A very substantial proportion of the yarns used in Canada has to be imported, and the existing duty on British yarns is to be abolished. Owing to the dry atmosphere in Canada it is impossible to spin yarns there at all comparable with West Riding yarns, and the fact that the latter are to be free will no doubt increase yarn exports from this country to the Dominion.
With respect to that one observation, may I venture further to point out that the memoranda submitted to the tariff board by the British and French textile manufacturers are, one would say, not intended perhaps to influence public opinion, and yet they in terms state that in their view no case has been made out. For instance, with regard to one of these matters that is dealt with in the tariff, that is the duties on cut pile fabrics of mohair, wool,

As this is rather at variance with the general principle of the revisions, it has caused some surprise, and protesting cables have been sent to Ottawa by private firms and also a joint protest from the Bradford and Huddersfield chambers of commerce. One private cable reads: Astonished to hear British cut pile fabrics of wool, mohair and alpaca are included under general wool tariff, thus raising duties by 10 per cent. This applies to mantle cloths and dress goods as well as furnishing fabrics. We submit that cut pile fabrics for dress goods wear are not manufactured in Canada. New change results in penalizing British manufacturers by reducing preference.
I doubt not that the minister may read to us to-night some of the cables he has received with reference to that matter. I believe this house represents the commonsense of the people of Canada, and that if possible, they desire to develop a woollen industry in the Dominion. I take it there is no gentleman, whether he is a protectionist, a free-trader, or anything else, that does not desire to have established in Canada by some means or other a strong, vigorous woollen textile industry. Ike need it. We should not be dependent upon other people for our supplies of wool or w'ool yarns; we should be in a position, if circumstances over which we have no control arise to interfere with our marine communications, where we have sheep sufficient to produce woo! to meet the demands upon our manufacturers by our people to supply them with clothing as well as with food.
Now, some of my friends think the woollen manufacturer desires an abnormal profit. I was very much struck by some of the observations I heard in the house, and I wrote to one of our leading textile manufacturers with reference to this matter. Let me quote his words:
I am satisfied with one cent a pair profit on footwear. Suppose I sell for 37J cents a pair, why should the same retail at 75 cents? kt e do not get it. It is the spread between us and the consumer.
Then he proceeds,
If I make a dollar a suit profit for the best cloth which can be bought for $15 to $16, say $20 trimmings included, and which when made up will sell for sixty or seventy dollars, I am satisfied.
Now, under those circumstances most of us, I think, had a strong hope that a tariff board, set up and properly equipped, would ascertain the facte and make a report to the Minister of Finance for submission to this house, that would enable every hon. member to conclude what would be necessary to be done to secure
IMr. Bennett.]
this industry to the Dominion. My observation has been, even when talking privately to some of my friends opposite, that they share with me a desire to establish a strong Canadian woollen industry. But they say: This protection, Mr. Bennett, is absurd. When I ask them why, they say:	Well, it is too
much to expect that an industry should be protected to such an extent, and it will mean that the country will be exploited by the manufacturers. That is the stock answer given. Against that there is the statement of the manufacturer to me, that he will be satisfied with a profit of a cent a pair on woollen socks. Would any man deny that as a reasonable profit? Says this manufacturer : Give me only a dollar profit on any suit I produce, and I am satisfied. That cannot under any circumstances, be said to be exploitation.
Then what should the minister have given to us? He has revised this schedule; he has put yam upon the free list. That is done at the instance of people wfio do not live in Canada, and it gratifies them because it means their looms will work while ours are idle. I do not yield to any man in my regard for the mother country and for the people who live there, but my first concern as a legislator must always be this country-Canada.	I am untrue to my position if my first concern is not Canada. And if I find looms working in Bradford and idle in Almonte, and the reason is in the action taken by this parliament, to which action I am a party, I have been untrue to this country. That is my submission to my friends opposite.
Now, is it a fact that our looms are idle? I have mentioned that more than half of the looms we have in this country are idle, and that there is increased activity in the looms of other countries by reason of the legislation the minister is putting on the statute books. If this be so, we have failed lamentably to discharge our duties as Canadians. I say it without offence, and I ask my friends opposite if it is not true. If we can protect our people against exploitation, and at the same time develop the woollen industry of Canada, if we can increase our flocks-which have been the foundation of national wealth since the days of Abraham-then let us do it. We cannot lower the standard of wages nor the type of living of our people, and we live in a cold country where woollen clothing is necessary. Is it beyond the reach of Canadian statesmen to attain this end? Is it beyond their capacity to accomplish this object? Let us for a moment forget these shibboleths of the past, let us forget the

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
terms, free trade, protection, low tariff, high tariff, with which, as the Minister of Finance said in Winnipeg, we play at election times; let us forget them and recall to our minds that we are concerned with the fate of a great Canadian industry that is threatened with absolute destruction. Not in its entirety- they will all tell you that-because those of our mills that have always beenl importing yarns will be able to do better than they ever did but the mill that has a million dollars invested in machinery to spin woollen yarns will find that machinery idle, while its owner will have the melancholy satisfaction of seeing a corresponding activity, three thousand miles away, in the spinning machinery of another country. That is the duty of Canadian statesmen that is the duty of any Canadian government-to conserve Canadian industry.
This tariff seems to have been moulded by the woollen manufacturers of Bradford and Huddersfield and the textile manufacturers of France rather than by Canadians for Canadians. I concede the right of every man who may be affected to present his views to a tariff board whether in this or any other country. 1 recall that when the cattle embargo was in force against us during the war it was discussed by Canadians in England, certain representations having been made at the time which we contended should be oarried into effect. As I say, I concede the right of interested parties to express their opinions as they see fit. But it is the duty of any man occupying the position I hold, without power to change or modify in any respect the schedules now under consideration, to indicate the danger to which the country is exposed. I know it is futile to appeal to the minister to change his schedules, and in any event, if he does determine upon any change, he does so in compliance with the views of his supporters behind him; and then seeks to blame us on this side for the simple reason that such a procedure makes better reading for the manufacturers. But does the Minister of Finance really believe that anyone is deceived by that sort of thing? Let me assure him, Mr. Chairman, that picayune, peanut politics of this description is precisely the thing that discredits the action of any minister in charge of tariff revision. The idea of saying to a free parliament, after striking out an item the other evening because some of his supporters told him he had to do so, " the opposition must shoulder the responsibility!" Having acted on the request of his own supporters, he turns to us and says, " You are to -blame; go and tell your friends the manufacturers what you have done Is not 56103-103
that sort of thing calculated to make parliament a byword among the people? Everyone saw the play and understood it. Who was deceived? No one, and least of all the people most vitally affected.
I presume it is too late to endeavour to induce the minister to alter or change his plans, but at least we can point out the facts and place the responsibility where it belongs. We can place the responsibility on the government of the day-a government which is not at all concerned about the development of this great industry but which, apparently, is bent upon pleasing people who reside far distant from here, yielding to the importunities and demands made upon it, as indicated in the Textile Argus and elsewhere. It is much easier for the government to do this than courageously to say, as they said in the United States, "We intend to impose high tariffs for the moment in order to encourage the industry and put it on its feet. We intend to control the situation and as circumstances change we shall be able to modify our tariff to suit those changing conditions". At any rate, we on this side shall have to content ourselves with pointing out the facts and leaving the responsibility with those who have incurred it for the state of affairs to which I have made reference and which is reflected in the census taken during the first three weeks of January of this year, in anticipation of the very action that has been taken.
It is not a pleasant thing for one to have to speak in this way with respect to these items under consideration; it is not pleasant to contemplate the injustice which will result from legislation thus enacted. It is all very well to say that free yarns will mean cheaper goods. But I would remind my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that utter dependence upon others operating great distances away has been the undoing of every state of importance; at any rate it has been the ruin of all the states of which I have read in history. Copper is an illustration: what is happening to-day in regard to that industry? What was the state of affairs during the war in relation to copper and zinc? Before the United States went into the war they were able to say to the nations of the world, "There is our price; you pay it or die". Is it worth while to have this country independent? Is it worth while to raise it to the level of sheer independence and make its people economically free? We did this during the war. We entered into a contract with the late Lord Rhondda by which it was agreed that a higher price by a half cent per pound should be paid us for copper

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
for war purposes if we would develop our copper industry. The United States then raised the price of zinc to 44 cents a pound; that was their answer, before they came into the war, to the assertion of economic independence on the part of the empire and its allies. And in the woollen industry-upon which our life depends in winter-shall we be dependent or independent? Shall we raise vast flocks of sheep, nine, ten, twenty millions, or shall we continue to import mutton from New Zealand? That is the question. With the greatest markets open to us, shall we extend our foreign trade or not? You say it does not require a tariff? I say it requires the use of every tool or implement that parliament has at hand to safeguard the industry. To me it is perfectly indifferent whether it be a tariff, a bonus, a bounty, a drawback or an export duty; I insist that we use the instruments we have for one purpose and one purpose only, namely, to make this country economically independent. Failure to do this is failure to grasp the opportunities that 'Providence has given us. Is it not a disgrace that a country such as this should be content to raise three million sheep? Those with whom I have discussed the matter understand quite well that in the great reaches of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, in the far west, in the prairie provinces and in British Columbia, a very considerable industry could be developed if we had the courage. And this country has the courage. I say to the Minister of Finance that if only he would take his courage in his hands those who sit behind him would rally to his support, because although, by profession, they are free traders in the west, in practice they are ready to utilize every instrument or tool that can be pressed into service to make this country great and strong. I am sure that if hon. gentlemen opposite thoroughly appreciated the situation, if the facts were properly put before them by the tariff board and by the minister, so that they could draw their inferences as well as he, they would understand the importance of the industry and be prepared to support it. I can only content myself with protesting against these measures which threaten the economic independence of the country and spell ruin to millions of capital invested in the manufacture of yarns in Canada.

I do not
propose to deal with this matter at great length, but I must congratulate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) on the eloquent plea he has just made. I have heard him on many occasions but rarely has he been in such
fMr. Bennett.]
excellent form and apparently so logical. Let me say, however, that in my opinion he destroyed the force of his speech by the last statement or two he made. The opinion he expressed is one he sincerely holds and believes in, but the idea that it is possible to make any nation economically independent is madness; it is a fallacy of the crassest kind. We can no more make Canada economically independent than the United States has been able to make the United States economically independent. It is a dream, the phantasy of a mind warped by convictions sincerely held in the wrong direction.
The leader of the opposition spoke about the destruction of this industry and he used several other trenchant phrases to emphasize the disaster which was rapidly overtaking it. Now there may be depression in the woollen industry; I sincerely believe there has been some depression in the last two years. But may I point out something that has been so far overlooked. So far as I have been able to ascertain-and in this regard I am rather slightly better able to know what I am talking about-women to-day do not wear wool, or they wear as little as possible. I happened to be travelling in eastern Canada last November and I visited some splendid woollen mills in the maritime provinces. In the Moncton mill I found that the manufacturers were more and more turning their attention to the manufacture of rayon mixtures. It is the introduction of rayon and artificial silks and material of that kind which attracts the ladies-I do not blame them-that has operated against the past profits of the woollen industry. That is one point that has not yet been noted. I do not think it can be stressed too heavily and it is one factor that has rather tended to lower the profits of these companies. But I would say this to the leader of the opposition and to those on his side who are so deeply concerned in this matter. I can produce proof to this house to-night that the woollen industry in Canada is not in bad shape, that it is not suffering seriously and that it is not likely to be destroyed. The best proof I can find is the action which has just been taken by one of the British woollen manufacturers, who has declared his intention to tear down his entire plant in Bradford, to which city my hon. friend referred, and bring the plant to Canada to manufacture wool here. The discussion on the wool item has taken rather a wide range and we are discussing under item number 549 practically all the wool items. Perhaps this may have the effect of shortening the discussion in the end. There is only one aspect of the wool business with which I am particularly concerned and that is in respect to the removal of the duty from woollen yarns, number forty and finer, which are manufactured to a large extent by an important firm in the riding which I have the honour to represent.
Until the present budget introduced by the Minister of Finance, worsted yarns were entitled to a protection of 12i per cent from Great Britain, 17i per cent on the intermediate tariff, and 22$ per cent on the general tariff; but as all worsted yarns which are imported come from Great Britain, we are not concerned very much with either the intermediate or the general tariff. The protection against worsted yams coming from Great Britain has now been removed, and they have been placed upon the free list. The result as regards the industry which I have in mind will be, I think, practically to close it up. It is an industry engaged altogether in the spinning of worsted yarns. There is, in connection with the woollen schedules in the customs tariff, a bit of history which perhaps it would be well to remember. The first tariff by a Liberal government-I do not mean away back in the days of Alexander Mackenzie, but in the Laurier-Fielding regime-was introduced into this house in 1S97. I think no change was made in the then existing duties on woollens, but there was in that tariff a provision which had a great effect upon the trade. For the first time Mr. Fielding introduced the British preference, granting for the first year, I think a discount of 12$ per cent; for the second year 25 per cent, and in the year 1900 the preference was increased to 33^ per cent. I well remember in the year 1902 going with a deputation of woollen men
*^lr. Evans.]
who came to Ottawa to interview Mr. Fielding, who was at that time Minister of Finance. They objected that the reduction of one-third of the tariff in favour of Great Britain brought about a situation under which they could not compete. Mr. Fielding took a reasonable and business-like view of the situation. He said' that he would have an inquiry made at once into the whole question, and within the next two years an inquiry was held and a report made to Mr. Fielding. As a result of that inquiry and report there will be found in' the Tariff Act of 1904 a clause that manufactured woollen goods-I am not now talking of yams-should enjoy a net protection of thirty per cent, notwithstanding any preferences, and the woollen trade enjoyed a protection of 30 per cent net from that day until the year 1923. Under a protection of 30 per cent the woollen trade prospered in Canada.
Prior to that time all worsted yarns came in free; but it was felt not only among the trade but among the good people of Canada in general that if we were able in this country to produce a very creditable cloth, a splendid woven cloth, it was strange that we' did not complete the fabrication; that we did not go back to the basis and make the yarns. If they could do it in England or in other countries, we could do it in Canada, so a deputation again called on Mr. Fielding and I again accompanied them. We met Mr. Fielding, the late Mr. Paterson and the late Sir Richard Cartwright, and my recollection is that His Honour, the present Speaker, was one of the ministers who received us. They laid their case before Mr. Fielding for the manufacture of worsted yarns in Canada. He' heard them patiently; he considered the whole situation, and I think he again ordered an inquiry. My recollection is that he sent someone over to Bradford to make a full inquiry into conditions which prevailed there with the idea of ascertaining why, if they could successfully make yarns in Bradford, we could not do the same thing in Canada. At all events in the session of 1907, when the main Fielding tariff was introduced into this parliament, Mr. Fielding granted the worsted yam manufacturers a tariff of 12^ per cent British preference, 17i per cent intermediate and 20 per cent general. Why did he do this? He did it in order to start the yarn industry in Canada. A number of mills which were in the habit of weaving cloths, immediately installed machinery to spin worsted yarn.
Worsted yarn, as a matter of fact, cannot or has not been made solely of Canadian wool. Canadian wool is not considered fine enough

to make the finer qualities of worsted yam. A percentage of it is used for that purpose. Some mill men tell me they use 15 per cent; others have told me they use as high as 20 per cent; but I think 15 per cent would probably be a fair average, and the rest of the raw yarn is imported, mixed with the Canadian yam and spun in the Canadian mills. Almost all the woven cloth manufacturers have established spinning plants in their own works. One or two have not done so, but in my riding a very extensive plant exists which does not make cloth, which exists only upon the spinning of worsted yams which it sells to manufacturers of cloth, ladies' garments, carpets, automobile interiors, plushes and the like. It is absolutely dependent upon that trade. It employs over 200 hands. It uses, say, 15 per cent of Canadian wool and 85 per cent of imported wool. All the preliminary processes are gone through in the Canadian mill-the scouring, the picking, the carding, the gilling, the spinning and the twisting-and while it is not altogether male labour that is employed in that work, the largest proportion of the employees are heads of families. This mill has been in operation since about the year 1907 or 1908, and it has gradually worked up a satisfactory and extensive business in Canada. It was started when the Liberal tariff of 1907 was passed by this house, giving a 12,1 per cent protection as against the importation of yarns from Great Britain. Why cannot this industry exist without that protection, may be asked, and what does the protection amount to? It cannot exist without protection because of the difference between the wages paid in Bradford, England, and the wages paid in Guelph, Canada, where this mill is situated. I notice that there is a difference between the statements made in regard to wages by the representatives of the Bradford and Huddersfield mills and the representatives of the Canadian mills. If you will read the statements that were made before the tariff board, you will note that the Canadian mill men say that the difference is as between sixty cents and one dollar; that is, that when sixty cents is paid in Bradford for wages, one dollar is paid in Canada. Some of them put it at fifty-nine cents, others at sixty cents. But the representatives from Yorkshire, who desire to gain the Canadian market for their own goods, say that the difference is as between $1 and $1.37. But whoever may be 'correct, the duty is only 12j per cent-not very much protection is it, Mr. Minister?
Now what does that duty amount to in regard to the cloth manufactured from worsted yams? To-day one pound of worsted yam
sells in Bradford at $1.25 and a 12-J per cent duty on that would make a duty of about sixteen cents a pound. One pound of that yarn goes to a yard of cloth. One manufacturer said you can average it at one and one-eighth pounds to the yard, but for my purposes one pound is easier to figure. Taking three and one-half yards of woven cloth to one suit of clothes, the protection amounts to about 56 cents on the yam that goes into a suit of clothes. That suit will retail at forty or fifty or sixty dollars, and 56 cents is the amount of protection on the yam in that suit. Yet that protection keeps hundreds and hundreds of men, and women too, working in the Dominion of Canada. The amount of duty involved is so small, so negligible, that it has no effect whatever upon the ultimate price which is charged for that suit of clothes. In the letter read by my hon. leader to-night a manufacturer states that if he could get a profit of one dollar a suit he would be satisfied. I know manufacturers in the county of Waterloo who say that if they could get fifty cents a suit they would be satisfied. Ten or twelve cents a yard they count as their profit on many lines of materials. Now is the duty of 56 cents on a forty or fifty or sixty dollar suit of clothes a burden on the people? I will tell the minister that it is not nearly as great a burden as is the sales tax. He has kept the three per cent sales tax on the sixty dollar suit. That is about three times as much as the customs duty, if the duty is to be considered a tax. This is the proposal of the Finance minister who succeeded Mr. Fielding, who established the worsted spinning industry in Canada by his tariff. These men were encouraged to invest their money in this industry in Canada, and they have invested tremendous amounts. I do not know whether there are other mills exclusively engaged in manufacturing worsted yarns as is the mill in Guelph, but I know that it has received a blow from which it is doubtful if it can recover. Already orders are being cancelled, and where are they being placed? They are being placed in Bradford. One-third of the output of the Guelph factory goes where? .To the Oriental Company in Oshawa, for plush for automobiles. They will not buy Canadian worsted yam in the future. They are going to buy it in Bradford now that it has been placed on the free list. I grant that the Oriental Company are going to be directly benefited to some extent by this proposal of the minister, but on the other hand it is a tremendous injury to the worsted spinning industry, which was established under the Liberal tariff of 1907.

that the bon. member for Hamilton will agree with that, and if the workers across the country were definitely assured that the protection which is extended to industry meant protection for them in respect of their wages and working conditions generally, a great many more would be inclined1 to favour that protection.
* Mr. BELL (Hamilton):	Hear, hear.

At the present time, however, they are not definitely assured of that; they are not guaranteed it. The figures I have read show that in practice they have not received that protection. I appeal, therefore, to the Minister of Finance, if he continues the policy of protection, to make sure that the workers will receive some share of that protection. No doubt there are certain peculiar conditions that might make some protection necessary for a time in special

industries, but the minister should first lay down the condition, in granting favours along this line, that a fair wage for all employees of these concerns Shall be guaranteed.

I am surprised at the narrow vision of hon. members to my left with regard to the future of this country. I cannot conceive how anyone can think it impossible for Canada to become economically independent. If there is any country in the world-any young country especially-that ought to become economically independent that country is Canada. We have everything to enable us to attain that independence. We have a large extent of territory, great natural resources of all kinds, a climate that produces the best type of people, and a people who can make the best use of the resources at their command. There is no reason, therefore, why this Dominion should not become one of the greatest nations of the world. I do not say that we can be independent on every score; there are certain things which we must necessarily obtain from outside, just as every other country must depend upon foreign sources for some of its requirements. The United States is economically independent, but the United States draws some of its supplies from without. If my hon. friend from Rosetown (Mr. Evans) had his way he would grow nothing but wheat in Canada, selling it in the markets of the world and getting his manufactured products from abroad. The result would be that he would turn Canada into nothing but an agricultural country. But we know that no country which was purely agricultural ever became great. Industry and agriculture must go hand in hand and develop together.
I have only a few remarks to make in regard to the woollen industry. I have previously stated that in my opinion the Minister of Finance was pointing his tariff revisions at industry in Ontario, and in support of this statement I have a few figures to submit. In the woollen industry in Canada in the year 1925 there were 119 plants as against 127 in 1924. Of these 119 plants producing in 1925, eighty-six were located in Ontario and they produced 80 per cent of the goods manufactured by the industry in the whole country. In 1923 the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding increased the British preference by 10 per cent. In 1922 we imported $196,000 worth of blankets and in 1926, as a result of that 10 per cent increase in the British preference, those blanket imports had risen to $601,000. In knitted goods we imported in 1922, $403,000, and in 1926, $769,000, the in-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
crease being attributable to the increase in the British preference. In socks and stockings, we imported in 1922, $1,371,000 and in 1926, $2,555,000-a considerable increase in that period. Taking our total wool products, our imports both dutiable and free amounted in 1922 to $35,000,000 and in 1926 to $46,000,000. This increase was due to the increase of 10 per cent in the British preference, which is a comparatively slight addition.
Now I turn to different sections of the woollen industry and I find similar conditions existing in Canada. Let us take the woollen cloth mills. In 1924 there were sixty of these mills in Canada, of which forty-five operated in Ontario. In 1925 there were fifty-seven. The capital invested in Canada in 1924 amounted to $22,551,000 and in 1925, $21,342,000. The wages in 1925 amounted to $3,913,000, Of the fifty-seven mills operating in Canada in 1925, forty-two were located in Ontario, and the capital in Ontario was $18,128,132 out of a total for the whole country of $21,342,000. The number of employees in Ontario in that year was 3,582 out of a total in all Canada of 4,426; and the wages paid in Ontario amounted to $3,331,000 out of a total I have already mentioned of $3,913,000. This shows the extent to which the woollen industry operates in Ontario in comparison with the rest of the country. Yet these are the industries which are being hit by the Minister of Finance in his budget.
Next I take woollen yarn mills in Canada. I am particularly interested in the woollen yarn business inasmuch as the industry operates in my county. In 1923 we had nineteen mills and in 1925 sixteen. The capital invested in 1923 was $9,279,416, and in 1925, $9,041,892. The greater part of these mills are in the province of Ontario, the capital invested in that province being $8,117,891. The number of employees in woollen yarn mills in all Canada in 1925 was 1,434, and of this number 1,100 employees were engaged in the mills of Ontario; while out of a total wage bill for the same year of $1,171,000 Ontario paid $899,946. Ontario furnished 80 per cent of the employees and 82 per cent of the production of woollen yam mills in 1925. But this particular industry is being severely attacked by the minister, and in one particular instance a mill in my own town will be practically put out of business. It is in the same position as the mill in the constituency of South Wellington. The effect of this budget will be severely felt, and the mill has already suffered a considerable loss in orders for the present year by reason of this tariff. They failed to meet the competition from the old country, and the manager is of the opinion that they will be unable to carry on. In a letter to me he states;
The entire problem is based purely on labour costs. We are led to understand that manufacturers in England can obtain experienced spinners for equivalent to $5 per week, whereas in this town under the minimum wage schedule, we are compelled to pay at least $10 per week.
If I recollect correctly, when the textile industry placed their case before the tariff board last year, the difference in labour costs between the industry in Canada and in England was around 70 per cent. It is a strange fact that with such a tremendous difference in producing costs, the price quoted by the English spinners to the Canadian knitter is only around 10 per cent below our price, which leads one to believe that the consumer in Canada is not reaping any benefit, equal in any way to the difference in the cost of production.
Although these mills will be almost put out of business because yarn is placed on the free list, the English spinners make a difference of only 10 per cent in their prices to the Canadian people, and if our mills cease production altogether the English spinners will control the market here and charge any price they wish. So we can reap no benefit from a reduction in these duties.
In connection with carpets, mats and rugs, in 1923 we had twenty-three factories producing these articles while in- 1925 there were only sixteen, a reduction of seven mills through the 10 per cent reduction in the British preference. Of this industry 99 per cent is in Ontario; the total production in 1925 for all Canada was $2,905,251, of w'hich the Ontario mills produced $2,874,967, leaving something over $26,000 produced in the rest of Canada. The capital invested in this industry throughout Canada amounts to $4,080,925, of which $4,059,837 is in Ontario, leaving $21,058 for the rest of Canada. These are the industries which are being injured under the present budget.
In 1925 we had thirty woollen cloth mills in Canada as against thirty-one in 1924; the capital decreased in 1925 as against 1924 by $127,942, while the number of employees decreased from 1,024 to 983. The province of Ontario supplied 64 per cent of the employees and paid 67 per cent of the wages, yet the Minister of Finance in presenting his budget fails entirely to grasp these conditions as far as this Dominion is concerned.
I wish to make a plea to the Minister of Finance that he reconsider his decision to place these yarns on the free list, and that he take into consideration the necessity that the spinning mills in this country receive the protection they need. I cannot see where these

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
reductions will lower the cost of the goods in Canada. If our industries can be kept working at high pressure, employing all their machinery, they will be able to have a larger production with a consequent reduction in price. Again I ask the minister to reconsider this decision with regard to placing yams on the free list.

I think we all agree that in Canada we want to maintain a reasonable standard of living for everyone. We do not want this to be a cheap country; we want good wages paid which will enable the worker to maintain his family in a proper manner. With that end in view we put legislation into effect many years ago for the purpose of keeping out certain cheap workers who could live very much cheaper than our own working peopie could live, and in so doing we felt that we were protecting our Canadian workmen. We adopted that many years ago and I quite agree with it, but if it is reasonable to do that is it not reasonable to protect our people against the products of cheap labour, manufactured in other countries? If it is reasonable to protect our own working people from the inroads of certain classes from across the Pacific, who work and live more cheaply than we do, what right have we to ask the producers of wool in this country to compete on a free trade basis with wool from South America, Mexico and other countries where labour is very much cheaper and living conditions are not to be compared with those in Canada?
I was very much interested in the comparison drawn by an hon. gentleman opposite between the conditions affecting sheep production in Australia and those which obtain in Canada. The hon. gentleman also referred to the area available in this country for the production of sheep and wool. It is true that in Australia, taken as a whole, they have a better climate for the production of sheep so far as cold is concerned, but on the other hand they have terrible droughts during which sheep die by the million. That condition prevailed during the past year in Queensland, so one condition is easily balanced by the other, and I think in the long run, taken over a period of years, we would probably have a slight advantage.

speechtext:
Does that apply to dairy
cattle?

I think dairy cattle are
usually kept on smaller farms. I am talking now about range sheep.
It does not effect butter.

In connection with the
question of wintering sheep in this country I might say that in those sections where it is necessary to feed sheep in winter, which is generally necessary because you must keep your breeding stock in good condition, it takes from two to three pounds of hay per day per head. That is when your range is covered with snow, but when you have plenty of winter range, that feeding is not necessary.
Then something was said about predatory animals. I have never heard that an English or Scotch dog would not chase a sheep. One hon. member made that statement, but although I have been identified with the stock business in this country for over half a century I never heard of that before. I have heard stories about them killing sheep in the old country, but of course I have no proof of that, 1 do know, however, that Canadian dogs will chase sheep whenever they feel like it. This gentleman also referred to a case where a sheep dog was taken before a magistrate in the state of Kentucky, I believe, but we always shoot our dogs first in British Columbia. Wo find that if we do not shoot them we take the risk that they will return some time in the early morning or during the night and destroy many sheep. Then we also have the coyote, and I must say that the coyote suffers no disadvantage on the Canadian side as compared with the United States. He knows nothing about tariffs or boundary lines; he crosses wherever sheep are to be secured.
Then I believe it was the hon. member for Bow River who said we were beginning to use rayon instead of wool. Coming from the banana belt as I do, from Victoria, British Columbia, I am not wearing rayon, and I am of the opinion that a man would have to be a trained Highlander for some length of time if he wanted to dress in rayon in this country, especially if he had to walk up parliament hill against a cold breeze in the winter time. The hon. member also said that the ladies were giving up wool and wearing rayon. I would advise him to put on his glasses on a cold day; I do not know whether they wear rayon or not, but they certainly wear wool on the outside.
I would like to refer again for a moment to the question of the limited area for the raising of sheep in Canada. I think that is a mistake. I can tell you exactly about British Columbia, where we have 160,000,000 acres of range land, 100,000,000 acres of what is known as timber range and 60,000,000 acres of open range. Of that area we are using only 6 per cent, and we buy 75 per cent of our meat outside the province. Compare that situation with the four states to our south, Oregon,

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
Washington, Idaho and Montana, and we find that while their total area is only a little larger than that of British Columbia they use 69.7 per cent of their range and supply themselves with their own meat, shipping their surplus to other places. What I should like to say is that some method should be adopted; at least a thorough investigation should be made as to the possibility of utilizing these hundreds of millions of acres of grass that are going to waste every year.
My good friend the Minister of Finance has stated, or hinted in a sort of shrewd Scotch wTay, that I had selected the figures that I presented to the house a little while ago. Let me point this out so as to get it on Hansard:	The tariff was taken off wool in
the United States in 1913. Whether they anticipated the war or not I do not know. At any rate wool was shipped in there in huge quantities. There was so much of it there that on May 27, 1921 they applied the tariff again, and then they applied the Ford-ney tariff on September 21, 1922. Now the sheep population of the United States on the 1st of January, 1922, was 36,186,000 head. On January 1, 1927, the number was 41,909,000. The wool clip in 1922 amounted to 263,713,000 pounds, shorn and pulled. The production in 1927 is estimated at 328,137,000 pounds. The duty on wool entering the United States is 31 cents per pound, clean content, the clean content being bone dry scoured weight plus 12 per cent for moisture regained. Scoured wool is subject to the same duty but without allowance for vegetable matter which may be contained. Such allowance is made when wool is imported in the grease or washed. The duty on dressed mutton is 2-i cents per pound. On dressed lamb the duty is 4 cents per pound. On live sheep and lambs there is a duty of $2 per head. This information, under date of March 1, 1928, is signed by John F. Bethune, secretary of the United States Tariff Commission. I may say that later figures indicate that in 1928 the sheep population increased to 44,455,000. I just wanted to bring these points to the attention of the house and to place these figures on Hansard for the use of the committee.

I should like to say a word
with regard to the last speaker's remarks. Like a good many other members I know very little about the wool tariff and I do not want to know. But the other night my hon. friend was speaking and he spoke of the neglected possibilities of sheep raising in British Columbia. Now he says: there are 160,000,000 acres in British Columbia adapted to sheep raising. I would not question the hon.
gentleman's figures, but I think they have been prepared by an optimist; they must have taken in a great deal of the lower parts of the mountains. We have Toughly three geographical divisions there. First there is a large portion of what you might call mountain. It is rocks, it may be valuable; in a lot of it there are probably minerals, but it certainly is of no use at all for grazing purposes. Then on the lower slopes which extend along the coast we have timber, but we could not graze sheep there and even if that were possible the wet climate would prevent it. So that the available land is confined to the more or less limited area in what is called the ranges. I think the hon. gentleman would agree that a great part of the land around and behind Kamloops is an illustration of the land of which I am speaking. The hon. gentleman complained the other night that measures are not adopted by which this range country in British Columbia could be utilized for sheep, and he complained bitterly of the amount of wool we are importing. I should like to mention a curious fact. It is quite true that we do import a lot of wool, but it is equally true that we export a large portion of the wool we do grow, for the reason that it is not suitable for the manufacture of cloth in this country. We do not raise the kind of wool that is required, and a great deal of the wool that is imported ostensibly from the United States really comes from Australia and is of a quality we do not grow here. Australia and New Zealand are sheep-growing countries and New Zealand is not subject to drought. Both countries have facilities for sheep growing, partly from long practice and partly from the manner in which they go about it. They run sheep cheaply, and their facilities for dipping and making them clean in every way are much better. When a man has 115,000 sheep on one farm, as I have seen there, it is reasonable to suppose that he has every modern appliance-scientific machinery, motive power for sheep shearing, conveniences for dipping, and things of that kind.
But I was talking about the range country around Kamloops. Now this is a fact within my own knowledge. A number of years ago the grazing land was thrown open, and of course the applicants were men who wanted to run both cattle and sheep, and we all know the bitter enmity there is between sheep men and cattle men. They used to murder each other down in the states because sheep kill a cattle range. They eat the grass closely, and men who are trying to run cattle do not want sheep on a cattle range. At the time these reservations were made, apparently the

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
political pull of the cattle men was dominant. It would not do to say that nothing but cattle should run on these ranges in British Columbia, that would not look well. So they said: You can run cattle and you can run sheep; but they put a little provision in that if anybody wanted to run sheep they would have to fence in the whole area with wire netting. That country is not rich in luxurious grass. It only carries very few sheep to the acre. I would rather say a number of acres to the sheep; and the idea of having the whole range fenced in with wire netting with a 35 per cent tariff on it meant that you could not run sheep at all. The cattle men did not say so, of course it would not have been politic, but matters were so arranged ;.hat the sheep man was not in the picture at all. He was confronted with a condition that he could not possibly economically comply with. So the cattle man had it all his own way. That is why we were not running sheep on the ranges round Kamloops. Time went on, and men saw the advantages and opportunities of running sheep, and they made application again and again to the government of Canada to have this regulation altered. They made application when the Union government was in power and they were refused. It has only been since this government came into power that these regulations have been changed. Since then sheep have been run in the neighbourhood of Kamloops and the number has increased enormously. It has increased in consequence of that little joker of which I have' spoken being taken out of the regulations. These are the reasons which perhaps explain why we do not grow more sheep in British Columbia. It is not a question of the tariff.
While I am on my feet I might mention- because it is something that came within my own knowledge-the question of competing *with English wool, and that if we had a tariff we would be able to do so. In some classes of this cloth we would not be able to compete, no matter what tariff there was. I was talking with a tailor last year and he gave me the name of a man who made up his mind to go into the manufacture of clothing in Canada-I think in Ontario, within a reasonable distance of Ottawa. He brought the machinery over from England and hired two dozen weavers to work in his mill so there would be no slip-up at all. He turned out excellent suits of clothes and distributed them amongst the tailors of this city; they could be sold at a better profit and for 810 less than other suits. But the man who told me this said there were no repeat orders and he wondered why, and he made it his busi-

ness to inquire. He found that the manufacturer had the same trouble-no repeat orders. The suit did not wear like the English cloth. The manufacturer had enough money invested that he had to find out what the trouble was, so he went to England and after considerable research he found that it was due to the kind of water that was used in connection with bleaching the cloth. I am not technically expert enough to explain why that was the case. There were some particular springs they had had for a few hundred years and they bleached the cloth after this water had been used with it. It was that that made the difference. No amount of tariff would have put the Canadian stock into the same class of goods with the English made article. The man wdio wanted to buy the superior article would have bought it; and the fact that he would have to pay more for it would not have given any advantage to the Canadian cloth manufacturer.

With regard to the
mountains in British Columbia, one of the advantages we have is that we can sell the scenery and still retain the mountains. The usual plan followed in the mountainous country is that of grazing sheep on the foothills where possible. I am not speaking of sheep confined in fences; I am speaking about one to three thousand sheep in charge of one or two men and two or three dogs. The sheep follow up immediately behind the snow on the mountain during the summer, using the succulent grasses for food, and in addition to that the sheep are fond of browsing. They eat many leaves when they can procure them. These mountains will carry many sheep.
With regard to the figures I gave a little earlier in the evening, those sheep I referred to were grown on a ranch within forty miles of Kamloops, the very country the hon. gentleman spoke about. They were raised on the Bill Roper Cherry Creek ranch and it was on that ranch the gentleman informed me that the sheep clipped ten pounds per head and the lambs in the fall weighed eighty pounds apiece. Anybody who knows anything about sheep will know that is a pretty good record under those conditions. We do not need any fences. While the cattlemen and sheepmen had a good deal of trouble in days gone by in British Columbia and south of the line, that is pretty well regulated now by grazing laws. Those figures which I have given, while they may appear optimistic, are Liberal figures, given out by the Liberal government in British Columbia, and while Liberal optimists may be rather scarce, those

are their figures and I am sure they are reasonably correct. I would not want to make any statement that I could not back up with figures. They will give the hon. gentleman what he wants to know.

What is the
breed of sheep to which the hon. gentleman referred?

Rambouillet crossed with
Hampshire.

A good deal has been said in the last few weeks by hon. gentlemen to my right with regard to the possibility of protecting our manufacturers without on the other hand letting them take advantage of it, that is, protecting them as regards the Canadian market, but not allowing them to increase the cost to the Canadian consumer. In view of the fact that notwithstanding all the debates in the House of Commons and the promises in the country, there has not been apparently any possibility of getting away from this policy of protection, I should like very much to see this matter explored. I think the most radical suggestion ever made by the farmers in the west was that people asking for protection should come before a committee of parliament and demonstrate to it their need for protection. I am quite sure that if the manufacturers of yam have a case against this revision of the tariff because they are losing some of the protection they had, we cannot
expect the people of western Canada, who are competing in the sale of their product in the markets of the world with cheap labour from all over the world, are readily going to waive their objections to the protective principle that they at least think has brought about dearer machinery, dearer clothing and higher costs of operations for them while not giving them any advantage as regards the sale of their finished product. But I believe they will be reasonable enough, if there is any possibility of protecting them against exploitation in the quality of the goods they must buy and the price they must pay, so that there is a basis there for doing what has so often been suggested should be done, namely, taking the tariff out of politics, taking away the disputes and the eternal arguments regarding it. But if that is done, it will have to be done in a thorough fashion and made so plain to the so-called free traders of the country that he who runs may read. I do not believe it should be beyond the capacity of our Canadian people and statesmen to ascertain whether it is possible to do that or not. A good many people have said something about a deal that I suggested between the people of the west and the Conservatives. I hope when hon. gentlemen refer to that, they will quote my speech on it, because I will stand back of it anywhere.

That was the
most radical suggestion made by the farmers of the west.

I will stand by that
speech in Saskatoon or any other place in Saskatchewan or Alberta-but it will have to be on a basis where we can provide protection for the farmers-and I cannot see so far how this can be done-and where the protected industries, in selling their goods, cannot take advantage of the farmers in price and in quality. But if there is a basis there, hon. gentlemen to my right and hon. gentlemen over there, who are supporting a protective tariff in the woollen schedules that is higher as far as my analysis goes than anything we have had before, ought to be anxious to explore that basis and to see if it is not possible to work out some scheme.

Wools, not specially provided for, and hair of the Angora goat, Cashmere goat, alpaca, and other like animals, imported in the grease or

washed, 31 cents per pound of clean content; imported in the scoured state, 31 cents per pound; imported on the skin, 30 cents per pound of clean content.
That is on wool. Paragraph 1109 of the United States tariff deals with woven fabrics, and reads:
Woven fabrics, weighing more than four ounces per square yard, wholly or in chief value of wool, valued at not more than 60 cents per pound. 24 cents per pound and 40 per centum ad valorem; valued at more than 60 cents but not more than 80 cents per pound, 37 cents per pound and 50 per centum ad valorem; valued at more than 80 cents but not more than $1.50 per pound, 45 cents per pound upon the wool Content thereof and 50 per centum ad valorem; valued at more than $1.50 per pound, 45 cents per pound upon the wool content thereof, and 50 per centum ad valorem.
That is the tariff of the United States, and I take it that hon. gentlemen directly opposite, of the official opposition, are arguing that Canada should approach that.
Not at all. Nobody suggested that.
