speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad to have that statement from my hon. friend, who I admit is as well posted as any hon. gentleman opposite on this question. It has been argued here that we would improve the condition of the woollen industry in Canada by putting a duty on wool. The figures show that in round numbers there are about 3,000,000 sheep in Canada with a population of about 10,000,000 people, while dn the United States the figures I have for 1926 show 40,000,000 sheep to a population of about 120,000,000 people. My hon. friend from Victoria gave figures for 192S which indicated a greater number of sheep, but hon. gentlemen will observe that relative to population there is just about the same number of sheep in each country, notwithstanding a duty of 31 cents a pound in the United States.
The woollen industry in the United States is not dn such a flourishing condition, for I observe that last year 58 woollen mills closed in the United States; nor is the woollen industry prosperous in Australia, where they grow the very best wool in the world. If any hon. gentleman feels that this is a good venture to go into in Australia, I might mention that the Australia Woollen Company's mills at Geelong have been advertised for sale for some years and according to the latest advices I have they have not yet found

a buyer. They were started by the government of Australia. It is true that in Australia they make excellent rugs and very good knitted wear, but they import tweeds just the same as we do in Canada. I will admit at once in regard to the piece goods branch of the woollen industry in Canada that it does seem to me that it should have a little more of the business. I observe in regard to piece goods that Canadian mills have just about 34 per cent of the business, but in knitted goods the Canadian mills have practically the whole business. If I had time before adjournment-
Can the minister give us the figures of the knitted goods importations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be glad to give that as we come to it. We have had a very interesting debate this evening, and if it has established one outstanding fact more than another it is the difficulty of making a tariff in this country that will suit everybody. If we had only to make a tariff to suit my hon. friend from Rosetown, that would be very easy, or if we had only to make a tariff in regard to knitted goods, in which my hon. friend from South Wellington is interested, that, too, would be very easy.
I am interested in woven goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is in the constituency of my hon. friend from South Wellington the only mill in Canada, I believe, that does exclusively custom work for yarn, and I will admit that the changes in the tariff may not be as helpful as they might be to that industry. But I want to put on record the statements that were made by the men in the industry in their application before the tariff board. They were asking for an upward revision of the tariff on behalf of the woollen industry, and I quote from a summary of their brief as presented regarding the decline of the industry:
The brief of the applicants as presented to the minister of February 1, 1927, stressed the prosperous condition of the industry and cited certain statistics compiled by the Department of Trade and Commerce, together with certain tariff changes made by parliament, with the expressed object of showing that less protection led to more depression. Inasmuch as the inquiry largely focussed upon the relation of the tariff to the apparent reduction in plants, the following paragraph from the brief is cited:
Then, what follows is from the brief presented by the manufacturers:
Between 1899 and 1907, 88 woollen and worsted mills, many of considerable size, closed their doors, the equipment including 129 cards and 559 looms. In 1907 the Canadian customs

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
tariff was divided into three classes, the British preferential tariff, which gave the lowest duty l ates, the intermediate tariff, which gave lower duty rates than before to countries making trade treaties with Canada, and the general tariff rates. Under this schedule by 1910 there were only 78 woollen and worsted mills in operation in Canada, operating 224 cards and 1,154 looms. This was 223 cards and 996 looms less than in 1899, or in other words, the industry had been practically cut in half in eleven years. This decline in the industry can only be attributed to the direct effect of reducing the duties.
What date is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am quoting from the brief presented by the manufacturers, February 1, 1927. Now I continue with the argument in answer to their brief:
Comparison of changes within the woollen and worsted industries of the United States, where tariff legislation has not run at all parallel to that of Canada, at once suggest itself as pertinent. For years the United States has followed what may perhaps be described not unfairly as a policy of high protection for its woollen manufacturers, although the benefits have been offset to a certain extent by the duties on wool.
And yet the course of the wollen and worsted industries in the United States has not been that of uninterrupted prosperity. The census of 1870 reported 2,891 woollen mills (as distinct from worsted mills) in operation, producing over $155,000,000 worth of fabrics. From that time until 1914, the census figures show a decrease each decade in the number of mills, and since 1879 a decrease in the value of products, except for the year 1904, when fashion temporarily gave a new impetus to woollen manufacture.
The census of 1914 reported 501 woollen mills with a product value of $103,815,905. The census of 1919 reported, according to the United States tariff commission, the first increase in the number of woollen mills in fifty years. 560 mills reporting a total output valued at $364,896,590. The census of 1921, however, again showed a decline in the number of plants and the value of products. After reviewing these figures, the United States tariff board comes to the following conclusions:
A review of the quantity of woven goods produced in the wollen mills in the last few decades is not encouraging to woollen manufacture. It is an industry that is on the decline if the per capita consumption is considered. When the production figures are studied it will be found that the number of establishments were reduced by more than one-half from 1900 to 1923. With the possible exception of overcoatings and certain types of cloakings, practically all other standard woollens have become somewhat less popular than formerly.
That is the statement of the tariff board in the United States where they do enjoy high protection. They continue:
Prior to 1925 the greatest volume of production was actually attained in 1909, and the successive censuses of 1914, 1919 and 1921 showed a trend downward. In 1923 there was a recovery of part of the ground lost. Omitting 56103-104
figures for partially manufactured articles, and for by-products and wastes, the production of woven goods by the worsted industry has been recorded by the bureau of the census as follows:
1909, 355,070,392 square yards.
1925, 275,105,188 square yards.
My hon. friend from Bow River must have been reading the report of the tariff commission of the United States, because they give practically the same reason that he advanced a few moments ago, that there is less woollen worn. I will come to that in a moment.
The per capita production, which is not materially different from the per capita consumption of domestic worsteds, was 3.92 square yards in 1909 and 2.38 in 1935, or a decrease of 39 per cent
That is the reason for some of the mills closing down. I am not going into the figures, as presented before the board, of the difference in costs. It was established that wages in Canada are higher than in the United Kingdom, and that they vary even in Canada in the different provinces. The relation of wages in Canada to those in the United Kingdom are as 160 to 100, the higher figure applying to Canada. In France and Italy the wages are as 40 to 50 of those in the United Kingdom. That is all I have to say in that regard.
During this debate we have had some criticism of the tariff board and of the representatives of the English mills appearing before the board.

Before the minister leaves that subject, was there at that time presented to the tariff board a comparison of the increase or decrease of the cotton business during the time that the wool business was decreasing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will look up that information and supply it to my hon. friend to-morrow. We have had some criticism of the tariff board, and also of the representatives of the English manufacturers coming before the board. I inquired carefully as to whether the trade agents of the British government had taken any active part before the tariff board, and I am told they had not. I made this inquiry because the instructions to our trade agents in different parts of the world, from this government and from the preceding government, is that they must be very careful not in any way to interfere with the making of tariffs in the countries where they are located. But that does not prevent individual Canadians, interested in manufacturing or selling, from time to time making representations to other governments.

Do they ever do it?

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I have a case in mind where representatives of certain Canadian manufacturing industries made representations to the British government through the Canadian board of trade in London, England. I recall certain Canadian manufacturers making representations to the government of South Africa, the government of Australia and the government of New Zealand, in an effort to secure certain privileges for Canadian goods which they thought they should enjoy in that market. At this very moment there are representatives of the agricultural industry in Washington. They recently appeared before the tariff board there. I do not find any fault with them. So we in Canada are not in a very good position to criticize the representatives of other countries for coming before our tariff board.
Are representatives of Canadian agriculture before the tariff board at Washington examining witnesses and in other ways taking an active part, or are they just watching the proceedings?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not say as to that. I know they are there looking after their interests in the hope that Canadian milk and cream will not be discriminated against in the United States market.
I do not think they are taking an active part.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Now, may I place on record these comments by the press of the country after the textile application had been heard by the tariff board? First, I quote from the Montreal Daily Star of January 6, 1928:
The respect for the tariff advisory board shown by the manufacturers and producers during the active life of that body within the past two years is an attitude which parliament and the government should emulate. The deliberate consideration of the merits of oases brought before the board has been in commendable contrast with the former hearings under pressure before the Minister of Finance or parliamentary committees. It is true the board is advisory and that adoption of policy still remains with the government of the day.
Now I quote from the Grain Growers' Guide of November 1, 1927:
The Canadian Maufacturers' Association maintains experts generally in support of tariff increases, and the Canadian Council of Agriculture and the Consumers' League generally represent the low tariff sentiment of the country. By thorough study of the problems before the board the representatives of these bodies are able to bring out all phases of the situation. The meetings are all public and open to the press and stenographic reports are taken of all evidence and cross-examination.
IMr. Chaplin.]
Next I read from the Toronto Financial Post of January 20, 1928:
It is undoubtedly a considerable improvement upon the former system, under which the Finance minister wasted most of his time listening to isolated and prejudiced pleas for tariff changes, and succeeded only in getting a superficial view of the problems before him.
Then the Winnipeg Free Press of January 10, 1928:
The value of this work canot easily be overestimated. In each case the position of the industry is examined in minute detail. Facts in regard to past financing, costs of production, efficiency of equipment, domestic and export prices, are revealed. Invariably the applications have been opposed, and opposition lias aided in laying bare prevailing conditions in each industry.
The Toronto Globe of January 14, 1928, has this comment, on the tariff advisory board:
It has held nearly one hundred hearings, has heard 41 pleas for upward revision of the tariff, others for lower tariff and sales tax adjustment; and those who have appeared before it testify to the thoroughness of its inquiries. It is not satisfied with less than a full presentation of both sides of every question, reinforced in many cases by independent investigations. Its disposition to be fair to all interested parties is conspicuous.
Then I have some comments upon the conduct of the woollen inquiry by some of those who appeared before the board. Mr. J. A. Bums, former president of the Canadian Woollen and Knit Goods Association, Toronto, said:
On behalf of the woollen manufacturers I would like to express our deep appreciation of the fair manner in which this investigation has been conducted.
From Mr. J. H. Shaw, manufacturers' agent in Montreal-and Mr. Shaw, by the way, not only represents the Canadian industry but is an importer-there comes the following:
Might I associate myself and my confreres with the expression of appreciation just given by Mr. Burns?
Then we have Mr. Hodgson of the Bradford Chamber of Commerce, Bradford, England :
May I be permitted to thank you and the board on behalf of Mr. Wood and myself for the very kind way in which you have received us and for your courteous consideration to us throughout a most intricate hearing.
I put this on record in justice to the board to show that there has been a full and fair enquiry. I am not sure that we can make much progress to-night but we have had a pretty full debate. I should like to meet my hon. friend from South Wellington, whose position I can appreciate. I fancy that if I had a woollen industry in my county

which was the only one in Canada I should feel pretty much as he does. Unfortunately, however, parliament must look to the country as a whole and consider every phase of industry, and while the Guelph Worsted Spinning Mill may not be helped it is believed, after a full inquiry, that the industry generally will benefit. It is true, as my hon. friend has said, that the company is selling most of its products to Oriental Textiles-

Not most; about a
third.

Well, they sell a good deal
to Oriental Textiles, and if there is a mill in Canada that might complain of Britishers coming before our tariff board it is not the Guelph mill, because I am advised that the owner of that mill is a gentleman who resides in England, coming here occasionally to look after the concern.
He is part owner.

with my hon. friend's argument, but this gentleman lives in England all the time and he is not in a position to attack others who appear before the board.

The importations have been
considerable-

Does not the minister
think that it would be better to have one hundred English gentlemen rather than one invest here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and that is what we are trying to do. The press this morning states that a mill will be established in Victoria, British Columbia, not only because of the change in the tariff but because of reduction of taxation in Canada.
Will that gentleman live in the old country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know, but his own statement is that he is moving out. As regards the statement that the spinning departments of Canadian mills will be closed down, it is possible that they may get a slight assistance in buying yams that they do not make.
I would point out that the dyeing department will also be affected, as many of these yarns are two strand, of different colours.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As regards the worsted cloth mills, there are nine without spinning plants, including plush and haircloth. These plants are: Oriental Textiles, La France Textiles, Canada Haircloth, Dominion Haircloth, Demetre Sault Ciriez, Dupont Textiles, Lockwoods Limited, Roxborough Textiles, Sykes & Taylor. I am told that these mills are unanimously in favour of the change. Those mills equipped with spinning plants are Paton, Canada Woollens, Rosamond and Forbes. Those who have gone carefully into the matter inform me that for every dollar in loss-if there is any loss-and every man put out of employment, there will be two dollars in profit and two men employed. The argument has been advanced to-night that the woollen industry has not been over prosperous. My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Anderson) quoted figures to show that in recent years there has been an increase in imports of woollen manufactured fabrics; but when you compare that statement with the statement I put on Hansard a few days ago, showing a considerable increase in the imports of wool, it seems to me that there is not very good ground for the allegation that Canada is not growing. If the country is not growing then the people living here are wearing more and better clothes, because there are more imports coming in both in wool and in finished products.
The tariff board, in considering how they could best help the industry-and everyone desires to help it-had two ways open to them: they could either put up the duty on the finished product or give a concession on the raw material required for the industry. They took the latter course and I believe it is sound. The people of Canada will be more inclined to endorse a policy of reducing the cost of production, making the goods for our people cheaper and better, than to adopt the policy of the United States of raising the tariff as high as Haman's gallows. We have the experience of the United States before us. Within recent years, since their high tariff has been put up, fifty-eight mills have

closed down there, and we know of one of the largest and best woollen mills in that country which has not paid dividends for the last two years.
There is one phase of the matter that has not been discussed. The mills will now obtain free machinery?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Has the minister considered the question of compensation to those mills that have paid large sums in duty into the treasury? I ask this question having regard to the elaborate statement of the Prime Minister, in speaking on the budget, with reference to the sales tax; he could not remove it because it would be unfair to those who had paid. Will the same principle apply to these mills in respect of their machinery on which they have paid duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has been a long time in parliament and he knows that duties that have been paid have never been refunded. This government is not yet through trying to settle the claim made by the automobile dealers in connection with the reduction of taxes made by a government of which my hon. friend was a supporter. That, I think, should satisfy him.

You should have had that cleaned up long ago.
